posts.title: What Is an SEO Audit? A Plain-English Checklist
posts.description: An SEO audit finds the technical and on-page problems that stop a page from ranking. Here is what it checks, in the order to fix things, with no jargon.

toc.text: What an audit can and can't tell you
The checklist, in the order to fix things
What to do with the results

posts.html:
An SEO audit is a health check for a web page. It looks at the page the way a search engine does and lists the problems that could stop it from being found, understood or shown in results. A good audit doesn't stop at problems. It tells you which ones matter most and how to fix each one.

You don't need to be technical to run one or act on it. Most fixes are a sentence in a title, a missing tag or a setting in your website builder.

What an audit can and can't tell you

An audit checks things you control on your own site: the code, the content structure and how the server responds. It can't see how strong your competitors are, how many websites link to you, or whether your content answers the search better than the page ranked first.

So think of the score as the floor, not the ceiling. A page with serious technical problems will struggle no matter how good it is. A page with a perfect score still needs useful content and some reputation to rank well.

The checklist, in the order to fix things

Fix problems from the top of this list down. The early items can stop a page from appearing in Google at all, while the later ones improve how well it does once it's there.

1. Can Google reach the page?

  • HTTP status 200. A page that returns 404 (not found) or 500 (server error) can't be indexed.
  • Not blocked by robots.txt. One wrong line in robots.txt can hide a whole section of a site. See our robots.txt guide.
  • No accidental noindex. A noindex tag tells Google to leave the page out of results. It's often left on by mistake after a site goes live.
  • HTTPS. Pages should load securely and plain http:// addresses should redirect to https://.

2. Can Google understand it?

  • A clear title tag of roughly 50 to 60 characters, with the main search phrase near the start.
  • One H1 heading that says what the page is about, followed by H2 and H3 headings in order.
  • A canonical tag pointing to the preferred address of the page, so copies don't compete with each other.
  • Alt text on images, describing what each image shows.
  • Structured data (schema) that labels your business, products or articles in a format machines read easily.

3. Will people click it?

  • A meta description that answers the search and gives a reason to click. Google doesn't always use it, but when it does it's your sales pitch in the results.
  • Open Graph tags so the link looks good when shared on WhatsApp, Facebook or LinkedIn.
  • A favicon, which Google shows next to your result on mobile.

4. Is it fast and mobile-friendly?

  • A mobile viewport tag, so the page fits phone screens.
  • Core Web Vitals: how quickly the main content appears (LCP), how fast the page reacts to taps (INP) and how much the layout jumps around (CLS). Our Core Web Vitals guide explains each one.
  • Compression and a quick server response, so the HTML arrives fast.

5. Is there enough to work with?

  • Enough useful text to answer the searcher's question. There's no magic word count, but a 40-word page rarely beats a thorough one.
  • Internal links to related pages on your site, so Google can find them and understands how they connect.
  • An XML sitemap listing the pages you want indexed.

How often to audit

Audit a page when you publish it, after any redesign or platform change, and whenever traffic drops suddenly. For an established site, a monthly check of your most important pages catches problems before they cost you visitors.

Changes made by someone else are a common cause of problems. A developer adds noindex to a staging site and it goes live, a plugin update changes your titles, or a new theme drops your schema. A quick audit after any change catches these.

What to do with the results

  1. Fix anything marked critical first. Blocked pages, error codes and noindex tags stop everything else from mattering.
  2. Work through the improvements page by page. Start with the pages that earn you money: your home page, main service or product pages and contact page.
  3. Re-audit after each change to confirm the fix worked.
  4. Ask Google to recrawl important pages through the URL Inspection tool in Google Search Console.

Run one now

The Rankdesk SEO audit checks a page against everything above, including Google's own PageSpeed data, in about 20 seconds. Each problem comes with a plain explanation and a link to the tool that writes the fix, already filled in with your site's details.

posts.title: How to Write Title Tags That Get Clicked
posts.description: The title tag is the blue headline in Google results. Learn the length, the word order and the formulas that win clicks, with before-and-after examples.
posts.html:
The title tag is the clickable blue headline people see in Google results. It's also the text in the browser tab and the default headline when someone shares your page. Of all the small changes you can make to a page, rewriting a weak title is often the one that makes the biggest difference to clicks.

Where the title tag lives

It sits in the <head> of the page's HTML:

<title>Pure Silk Sarees from Surat | Shree Textiles</title>

In WordPress, Shopify, Wix and most builders you don't edit code. You set it in an "SEO title" field, usually under the page settings or in a plugin such as Yoast or Rank Math.

How long should it be?

Google cuts titles that are wider than about 600 pixels on desktop. For most titles that is around 50 to 60 characters. Pixels matter more than characters, because wide letters such as W and M take more space than i or l. Write the important words first so a cut never removes them.

Google also rewrites titles that are too long, stuffed with keywords or don't match the page. Keeping yours clear and accurate makes it far more likely Google shows it as written.

A formula that works

For most pages, use this order:

Main search phrase + what makes you different + brand

  • Pure Silk Sarees from Surat | Shree Textiles
  • Bathroom Waterproofing in Ahmedabad, 5-Year Warranty | Bhanderi Buildcon
  • Free IP Address Lookup with City and ISP | IPLocator Tools

The search phrase goes first because people scan the start of each result for the words they typed. The brand goes last because it matters most to people who already know you.

Before and after

Before After
Home Wedding Photographer in Rajkot, Candid and Traditional
Products Stainless Steel Kitchen Sinks, Factory Prices
Blog Post 14 How to Choose a Water Purifier for Hard Water
Welcome to ABC Clinic Dental Clinic in Vadodara Open Sunday, ABC Dental

Every "after" tells the searcher what they'll get before they click.

Rules worth following

  • Make every title unique. If ten pages share one title, Google can't tell which to show.
  • Match the page. If the title promises prices, the page should show prices. A mismatch leads to quick back-clicks and Google may rewrite the title.
  • Write for people. "Saree, sarees, buy saree, saree online" reads as spam. One natural phrase is enough.
  • Use numbers and specifics where they're true: "5-year warranty", "open Sunday", "12 examples".
  • Separate parts with a pipe | or a dash. Both work. Pick one and use it across the site.

Titles for different page types

  • Home page: what you do and where, then the brand. Interior Designers in Surat for Homes and Offices | Studio Nine
  • Product page: the product name as people search it, a key detail, then the brand.
  • Service page: the service, the city and a differentiator.
  • Blog post: the question or promise. How to Remove Hard Water Stains from Tiles
  • Category page: the category in plural with a qualifier. Cotton Kurtis for Women, Under ₹999

The title and the H1

The H1 is the main heading on the page itself. It can match the title tag or be a slightly longer, friendlier version. What matters is that both describe the same topic. See our guide to headings for how they fit together.

Check how it looks

Before publishing, preview the title as it'll appear in results. The Rankdesk meta tag generator measures the real pixel width, shows the desktop and mobile results, and gives you the finished tag to copy. Pair it with a strong meta description and you've written the whole search result.

posts.title: Google Business Profile: A Complete Setup Guide for Indian Businesses
posts.seoTitle: Google Business Profile Setup Guide for Indian Businesses
posts.description: Your Google Business Profile decides how you appear on Maps and local results. Set it up properly, from category and photos to posts and replies.

toc.text: Step 1: Claim or create the profile
Step 3: Get the core details right

posts.html:
When someone nearby searches for "saree shop near me" or "plumber in Navrangpura", the first thing they usually see is a map with three businesses under it. Those listings come from Google Business Profile, a free listing that every shop, clinic, office and service business should claim.

For many local businesses, the profile brings more calls and visits than the website does. Here is how to set it up properly.

Step 1: Claim or create the profile

  1. Go to google.com/business and sign in with the Google account you want to manage the business from. Use a business account rather than a personal one if several people will help.
  2. Search for your business name. If it already exists (customers sometimes add businesses to Maps), claim it. If not, create it.
  3. Choose whether customers visit you at a location, you visit them, or both. A business that serves customers at their address, like a carpenter, can hide its street address and show a service area instead.

Step 2: Verify it

Google needs to confirm you run the business before the profile goes live in full. It offers whichever methods it considers right for your business, which can include a video recording of your premises and signage, a phone or SMS code, email, or a postcard. Follow the instructions exactly. A video, for example, usually needs to show your signboard, the location and proof you manage it, such as opening the shop.

Don't change your name, address or category while verification is pending, as it can restart the process.

Step 3: Get the core details right

  • Business name: your real name as it appears on your signboard. Adding keywords, such as "Shree Textiles Best Saree Shop Surat", breaks Google's rules and can get the profile suspended.
  • Primary category: the single most important ranking setting. Pick the most specific category that describes your main business, such as "Saree shop" rather than "Clothing store". Add a few secondary categories for other services.
  • Address and pin: check that the map pin sits exactly on your entrance.
  • Phone and website: use a number that is answered during business hours.
  • Hours: include special hours for Diwali and other holidays. Wrong hours lead to angry reviews.

Use exactly the same name, address and phone number everywhere online. Our NAP consistency guide explains why.

Step 4: Fill everything else

Profiles with more detail tend to get more engagement:

  • Description: 750 characters explaining what you do, who for and where. Write it for customers, naturally.
  • Products and services: add each main service with a short description and, where sensible, a price.
  • Attributes: for example wheelchair access, women-owned, online appointments or delivery.
  • Photos: your shopfront from the street (so people recognise it), inside, your team, products and finished work. Real photos beat stock images. Add new ones every month.

Step 5: Reviews

Reviews influence both rankings and whether people choose you. Ask every happy customer, make it easy with your review link, and reply to every review, good or bad. Our guide to getting more Google reviews covers what is allowed and what is not.

Step 6: Keep it active

  • Posts: share offers, new stock, events and updates. They appear on your profile and show you're active.
  • Questions and answers: customers can ask questions on your profile. Answer them quickly and accurately.
  • Messages and calls: respond fast. Slow replies lose customers to the next listing.

Connect it to your website

Your profile and website support each other. Link the profile to the most relevant page, usually your home page or a location page. On the website, show the same name, address and phone, embed a map on the contact page, and add LocalBusiness schema so search engines can match the two.

Common mistakes

  • Keyword-stuffed business names
  • Wrong primary category
  • A virtual office or PO box as the address (not allowed)
  • Several profiles for one location
  • Photos that are only logos or stock images
  • Never replying to reviews

Fix these and work through the local SEO checklist, and your profile will be in a strong position against competitors who set theirs up once and forgot about it.

posts.title: Schema Markup for Beginners: JSON-LD Without the Jargon
posts.description: Schema markup labels the facts on your page so search engines understand them. Learn what it is, which types matter and how to add it.

toc.text: The rules that keep you safe

posts.html:
Your page might say "Open Monday to Saturday, 10 to 7" and "★ 4.6 from 120 reviews". A person reads that instantly. A search engine sees words and has to guess which numbers are hours and which are a rating. Schema markup removes the guessing by labelling the facts in a format machines read directly.

What schema markup is

Schema is a shared vocabulary, published at schema.org and supported by Google, Bing and others. It has types such as LocalBusiness, Product, Article and FAQPage, and properties such as name, address, price and openingHours.

You add it to a page as a small block of code that visitors never see. The format Google recommends is JSON-LD, which looks like this:

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "LocalBusiness",
  "name": "Shree Textiles",
  "telephone": "+91-98765-43210",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "Ring Road Textile Market",
    "addressLocality": "Surat",
    "addressCountry": "IN"
  },
  "openingHours": "Mo-Sa 10:00-19:00"
}
</script>

It's just labelled facts: this is a local business, here is its name, phone, address and hours.

Why it's worth adding

  • Rich results. Some types can change how your result looks. Products can show price and stock, articles can show a larger image, and breadcrumbs replace the plain URL with a readable path.
  • Clearer understanding. Schema confirms which business, product or person a page is about, which helps search engines connect your website, your Google Business Profile and mentions elsewhere.
  • Future use. AI assistants and newer search features rely on structured information. Clean facts are easier for any system to use.

Schema isn't a direct ranking boost, and adding it doesn't guarantee a rich result. Google decides when to show them. But it removes ambiguity, and that rarely hurts.

The types most sites need

Type Use it on What it can do
Organization Home or about page Confirms your name, logo and social profiles
LocalBusiness Home or contact page of a physical business Address, hours, phone, location on the map
Product Product pages Price, availability and reviews in results
Article / BlogPosting Blog posts and news Headline, image, author and date
BreadcrumbList Most inner pages Shows the page's position in your site
FAQPage Genuine FAQ pages Limited rich results today (see our FAQ schema guide)

The rules that keep you safe

  1. Mark up only what's visible. If the schema says 4.8 stars, the page must show that rating. Hidden or invented data breaks Google's guidelines and can lead to a manual penalty.
  2. Be accurate. Prices, hours and stock status should match the page and stay up to date.
  3. Use the most specific type. Dentist or ClothingStore says more than LocalBusiness, and both inherit all the same properties.
  4. One clear main entity per page. A product page is about one product. Don't mark up every product on a category page as if each were the main one.

How to add it

  • WordPress: SEO plugins like Yoast and Rank Math add Organization, Article and Breadcrumb schema automatically. WooCommerce adds Product schema.
  • Shopify: most themes include Product schema. Check it with a validator before adding more, so you don't create duplicates.
  • Hand-coded sites: paste the JSON-LD block anywhere in the page, usually just before the closing </head> or </body> tag.

Test before and after

Run every page through Google's Rich Results Test to see which rich results it qualifies for, and the Schema Markup Validator to catch errors in any type. After publishing, Search Console reports schema problems across your whole site under its Enhancements section.

Build yours

The Rankdesk schema generator builds valid JSON-LD for local businesses, organizations, products, FAQs and articles. Enter your website and it fills the fields from your existing pages, so you only check and copy. For businesses with a shop or office, start with our LocalBusiness schema guide.

posts.title: Keyword Research for Beginners: From Seed Keyword to Content Plan
posts.seoTitle: Keyword Research for Beginners: Seed Keyword to Content Plan
posts.description: Find the words your customers actually type, judge which ones you can rank for, and turn them into a simple plan of pages with free tools.

toc.text: Step 1: Write down your seed keywords
Step 4: Judge whether you can rank
Step 6: Use the keyword well on the page

posts.html:
Keyword research means finding the words people type into Google when they're looking for what you offer, and deciding which of those searches each page on your site should answer. Done well, it stops you writing pages nobody searches for and shows you where the easy wins are.

You don't need expensive tools to start. You need your customers' language, a few free tools and a spreadsheet.

Step 1: Write down your seed keywords

Seed keywords are the basic names for what you sell or do, in the words customers use, not your internal jargon. A saree manufacturer might start with:

  • silk saree
  • banarasi saree
  • saree wholesale

A builder might start with "house construction", "bathroom waterproofing" and "home renovation". Ask your sales team or check WhatsApp enquiries. How customers describe their problem is gold.

Step 2: Expand each seed

Every seed has dozens of variations. They fall into four groups, and each needs a different kind of page:

  • Local: "silk saree shop in Surat", "waterproofing contractor near me"
  • Commercial (comparing): "best banarasi saree brands", "waterproofing vs tiling"
  • Transactional (ready to buy): "silk saree price", "buy banarasi saree online"
  • Informational (questions): "how to identify pure silk", "why does my bathroom wall get damp"

The Rankdesk keyword ideas tool generates all four groups from your seeds. Then add real searches from these free sources:

  • Google autocomplete: type your seed slowly and note the suggestions.
  • People also ask: the question boxes in results show what people want to know next.
  • Related searches: at the bottom of the results page.
  • Google Search Console: once your site has some traffic, the Performance report lists searches you already appear for.

Step 3: Check demand

Not every phrase is worth a page. To see whether people actually search a term:

  • Google Keyword Planner gives search volume ranges. It's inside Google Ads, but you don't have to run ads to use it.
  • Google Trends compares the popularity of a few terms and shows seasonal patterns, such as saree searches rising before wedding season.

Small numbers aren't a reason to skip a keyword. Ten searches a month from buyers ready to order can be worth more than a thousand from students.

Step 4: Judge whether you can rank

Search the keyword yourself and look at page one:

  • If it's full of huge national brands and marketplaces, a new site will struggle. Look for a longer, more specific version.
  • If you see small local businesses, forums or thin pages, you have a real chance.
  • Look at what kind of pages rank. If they're all guides, a product page won't rank there, and the reverse is true too. This is search intent, explained in our search intent guide.

New websites do best with long-tail keywords: longer, specific phrases with clear intent.

Step 5: Group keywords into pages

Put closely related keywords together. "Silk saree price", "pure silk saree cost" and "silk saree rate" are one intent, so they belong on one page. Creating a separate page for each leads to pages competing with each other.

A simple spreadsheet works:

Page Main keyword Related keywords Intent Exists?
/silk-sarees silk saree pure silk saree, silk saree price Transactional Yes, needs work
/blog/identify-pure-silk how to identify pure silk silk burn test, real vs fake silk Informational No
/surat-showroom saree shop in surat saree market surat Local No

Step 6: Use the keyword well on the page

For each page, use the main keyword:

  • in the title tag, near the start
  • in the H1 heading
  • in the first paragraph, naturally
  • in the URL, if you're creating a new page

Use the related keywords in H2 headings and body text where they fit. Don't repeat the main phrase over and over. Modern search understands synonyms and context, and stuffing reads badly.

Keep it going

Keyword research isn't a one-time job. Every few months, check Search Console for new searches you appear for, add pages for gaps, and improve pages that rank on page two. Small, steady improvements add up.

posts.title: Instagram SEO: How People Find Your Profile in Search
posts.description: Instagram search runs on keywords, not just hashtags. Learn where Instagram reads your words and how to set up your name, bio, captions and Reels to be found.

toc.text: Put a keyword in your name field
Write a bio for people and search
Reels: say it and show it

posts.html:
Many people now search Instagram the way they search Google. They type "bridal lehenga Ahmedabad" or "home bakery Surat" and browse the results. Instagram SEO means setting up your profile and posts so they appear in those searches.

The good news is that most of it is free and quick. The work is in using the right words in the right places.

Where Instagram reads your words

Instagram matches searches against several parts of your account:

  1. Username (@shreetextiles)
  2. Name field, the bold name on your profile
  3. Bio
  4. Captions, especially the first lines
  5. Hashtags
  6. Text on Reels and spoken words, which Instagram can read and transcribe
  7. Alt text on images
  8. Location tags

Put a keyword in your name field

The name field is searchable and separate from your username. Most businesses waste it by repeating their brand. Add what you do and where:

  • Shree Textiles | Silk Sarees Surat
  • Dr. Mehta | Dentist in Vadodara
  • Crumbs & Co | Home Bakery Ahmedabad

You have a limited number of characters, and Instagram restricts how often you can change the name, so choose carefully. The Rankdesk hashtag generator builds a name field and bio for you and shows the character count.

Write a bio for people and search

Your bio should answer three questions in a few short lines: what you offer, where, and what to do next.

Factory-direct pure silk sarees
📍 Surat, India · Ships across India
👉 DM for the wholesale price list

Read our Instagram bio guide for more examples by type of business.

Captions: lead with the keyword

Write captions the way people search. Instead of "New arrivals! 😍", try "New Banarasi silk sarees for the wedding season, handwoven in Varanasi". The first line also shows in the feed before "more", so it has to work for people too.

Keep it natural. A caption written only for search reads like spam, and people scroll past.

Hashtags still help, differently

Hashtags now act more like labels that tell Instagram what a post is about than a way to go viral. Instagram has been cutting back on how many hashtags it allows per post, so check the current limit in the app. A small, relevant set beats a block of thirty. Mix:

  • Niche tags for what the post shows: #banarasisaree
  • Local tags for where you are: #suratfashion
  • A branded tag for your business: #shreetextiles

Our hashtag guide covers how to choose them.

Reels: say it and show it

Instagram can read text on screen and transcribe speech in Reels. If your Reel is about "how to drape a silk saree", say those words and put them on screen in the first seconds. Add captions, which also help the many people watching without sound.

Alt text and location

  • Go to Advanced settings before posting and write alt text that describes the image: "Red Banarasi silk saree with gold zari border". It helps accessibility and search.
  • Tag your city or area on posts. Local searchers browse location pages.

Getting found in Google too

Instagram allows public posts from professional accounts to be shown in search engines such as Google. If you want this, check your account's privacy settings and keep the account public. Keyword-rich captions then help in both places.

Signals that matter beyond keywords

Keywords get you into the results. What keeps you there is how people react: saves, shares, comments, watch time on Reels and follows from your profile. Post regularly, reply to comments and DMs, and make content people want to keep. A searchable profile with nothing worth following won't grow.

A quick checklist

  • Keyword and city in your name field
  • Clear bio with offer, location and call to action
  • Keyword in the first line of each caption
  • A few relevant hashtags, rotated
  • Alt text and a location tag on every post
  • Spoken and on-screen keywords in Reels

posts.title: SEO for Small Businesses in India: Where to Start With No Budget
posts.seoTitle: SEO for Small Businesses in India: Start With No Budget
posts.description: A realistic plan for shops, manufacturers and service businesses to get found on Google without an agency, using free tools and a few hours a week.

toc.text: Week 2: Fix what blocks your website
Week 3: Write titles and descriptions that sell
Week 4: One page per service or product line

posts.html:
Most small business owners in India hear about SEO from agencies selling monthly packages. Plenty of what those packages do is work you can do yourself, if you know the order. This guide sets out a plan you can follow with free tools and a few hours a week.

Be realistic about time

SEO is slow. Fixing technical problems and setting up a Google Business Profile can bring results within weeks. Ranking new pages for competitive searches usually takes months. If you need customers this week, run ads alongside. SEO is what keeps bringing them in after the ads stop.

Week 1: Get found locally

If customers can visit you or you serve a city, this comes first. It's often the fastest return.

  1. Claim and complete your Google Business Profile. Follow our setup guide.
  2. Choose the right primary category and add real photos.
  3. Ask your ten most recent happy customers for a Google review.
  4. Make sure your name, address and phone are identical on your website, profile, JustDial, IndiaMART and social pages. See NAP consistency.

Week 2: Fix what blocks your website

Run your home page and main service or product pages through a free SEO audit. Fix anything marked critical:

  • pages returning errors
  • noindex tags left over from development
  • robots.txt blocking pages
  • the site not loading over HTTPS

Then add Google Search Console. It's free, tells you which searches you already appear for, and alerts you to problems.

Week 3: Write titles and descriptions that sell

Your home page title shouldn't be "Home". Each important page needs a unique title tag that says what you offer and where, and a meta description that gives a reason to click. This often lifts clicks from searches you already rank for, without ranking any higher.

Week 4: One page per service or product line

Many small business sites have one page listing everything. Google can't rank one page for twenty different searches. Create a separate page for each main service or product line, with:

  • a clear heading that matches how people search
  • what it is, who it's for, prices or a price range if you can share them
  • photos of your actual work or products
  • answers to the questions customers ask on the phone
  • a clear way to call or WhatsApp you

A builder might have separate pages for house construction, renovation, waterproofing and interior work. A textile maker might have pages for each fabric or saree style.

Month 2: Answer customer questions

Write down every question customers ask before buying: price, time, materials, how to choose, how to care for the product. Each good question can become a guide on your website. These pages attract people early in their decision and show you know your trade.

Use the keyword ideas tool to find the exact phrasing people search. Then check our keyword research guide.

Month 3 and on: Build reputation

Google trusts websites that other trusted websites mention. As a small business, you earn this through:

  • local business directories and trade associations
  • suppliers and partners linking to you
  • local news coverage of something you did
  • guest articles for trade publications

Avoid buying links. It breaks Google's rules, and cheap link packages often do more harm than good.

Don't forget Instagram and YouTube

Many Indian customers search Instagram and YouTube before Google. Set up your Instagram profile for search and, if you can, post short videos of your work. The same keywords you found for your website apply there too.

What to measure

Check these once a month:

  • Search Console: clicks, impressions and the searches you appear for
  • Google Business Profile: calls, direction requests and website clicks
  • Enquiries: ask every new customer how they found you

If the numbers rise slowly, the plan is working. If something drops suddenly, run an audit to see what changed.

When to hire help

Doing it yourself works well for the basics. Consider an expert when you're in a highly competitive market, when your site has serious technical problems you can't fix, or when your time is worth more running the business. Even then, knowing the basics helps you judge whether an agency is doing real work.

posts.title: Meta Descriptions: 12 Examples and a Simple Formula
posts.description: The meta description is your sales pitch under the search result. Use this formula and 12 examples for shops, services, tools and blog posts.
posts.html:
The meta description is the grey text under your blue title in Google results. It doesn't directly change where you rank, but it strongly affects whether people click. Think of it as a short advert for the page.

How long should it be?

Google trims descriptions that are too wide, usually somewhere around 150 to 160 characters on desktop and less on mobile. Put the most important information in the first 120 characters so it survives either way.

Will Google use mine?

Not always. Google often shows a different sentence from the page when it thinks that sentence matches the search better. You can't force it, but a clear, relevant description that matches the page's main topic is used far more often.

A simple formula

What the page offers + a detail that matters to the searcher + a reason to act

The details that matter are usually price, location, speed, proof or something free.

12 examples

Shops and products

  1. Silk sarees: "Pure Banarasi and Kanjivaram silk sarees direct from our Surat looms. Wholesale rates for dealers and delivery across India."
  2. Kitchen sinks: "Stainless steel kitchen sinks in 30+ sizes, with 10-year rust warranty. Factory prices, free delivery in Gujarat."
  3. Home bakery: "Eggless custom cakes in Ahmedabad, baked to order. Order on WhatsApp by 2 pm for same-day delivery."

Services

  1. Waterproofing: "Terrace and bathroom waterproofing in Ahmedabad with a 5-year written warranty. Free site inspection within 48 hours."
  2. Dentist: "Painless root canals, braces and implants in Vadodara. Open Sundays. Book online or call for an appointment today."
  3. CA firm: "GST registration, returns and income tax filing for small businesses in Rajkot. Fixed monthly fees, no surprises."

Tools and software

  1. IP lookup: "Find the city, country and internet provider of any IP address. Free, instant and no signup needed."
  2. Invoice app: "Create GST invoices on your phone in under a minute. Free for up to 50 invoices a month."
  3. SEO audit: "Check any page for title, meta tags, schema, speed and crawl problems. Free SEO audit with a fix list in 20 seconds."

Blog posts and guides

  1. How-to: "Learn the burn test, the ring test and four other ways to check whether a saree is pure silk before you buy."
  2. Comparison: "Waterproofing coating or tiling: we compare cost, lifespan and leak risk for Indian terraces, with real prices."
  3. Checklist: "A 20-point local SEO checklist for shops and service businesses, from Google Business Profile to reviews."

Notice that none of them repeat a keyword awkwardly, and every one gives the reader something specific.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving it empty. Google then picks any text from the page, often your menu or cookie notice.
  • Copying one description across many pages. Every page should have its own.
  • Keyword lists. "Sarees, silk sarees, buy sarees, sarees Surat" looks spammy and gets ignored.
  • Promising what the page doesn't deliver. People bounce back to the results, and Google notices pages that disappoint.
  • Quotes in the code. A double quote " inside the tag can cut it off. Use single quotes or rewrite.

Where to set it

In WordPress use the meta description field in Yoast, Rank Math or a similar plugin. Shopify and Wix have a search preview section on each page and product. In raw HTML it goes in the <head>:

<meta name="description" content="Pure Banarasi silk sarees direct from Surat looms...">

Preview it

Write your title tag and description together, because people read them as one. The Rankdesk meta tag generator shows both in a live Google preview with width meters, plus the WhatsApp and LinkedIn share card, and gives you the code to copy.

posts.title: Robots.txt Explained: How to Allow, Block and Test Crawlers
posts.description: Robots.txt tells crawlers where they can and cannot go on your site. Learn the syntax, safe examples, the mistakes that hide whole sites, and testing.
posts.html:
Robots.txt is a small text file at the root of your website, at yourdomain.com/robots.txt. Before a search engine crawls your pages, it reads this file to see which areas it's allowed to visit. Get it right and crawlers focus on the pages that matter. Get it wrong and you can hide your entire site from Google.

What it looks like

User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin
Disallow: /cart

Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml
  • User-agent says which crawler the rules apply to. * means all of them.
  • Disallow lists paths the crawler shouldn't visit.
  • Allow (optional) makes an exception inside a blocked path.
  • Sitemap tells crawlers where your XML sitemap is.

Paths match from the start. Disallow: /admin blocks /admin, /admin/settings and also /administration. Add a trailing slash, /admin/, if you only mean the folder.

What robots.txt is for

Use it to keep crawlers out of areas that have no value in search:

  • admin and login pages
  • cart, checkout and account pages
  • internal search result pages
  • filter and sort variations that create thousands of near-duplicate URLs
  • staging or test folders

For small sites, the file is often nearly empty, and that's fine. Allowing everything is a safe default.

What it's not for

Robots.txt doesn't remove pages from Google. It stops crawling, not indexing. If other pages link to a blocked URL, Google can still list it, usually with no description. To keep a page out of results, allow crawling and add a noindex tag. Our guide to noindex vs robots.txt explains this common confusion.

It's not security. The file is public, and anyone can read it. Never use it to "hide" private pages. Protect them with a password.

Mistakes that cause real damage

  1. Disallow: / blocks the whole website. Developers often add it to a staging site and forget to remove it at launch.
  2. Blocking CSS and JavaScript. Google renders pages like a browser. If it can't load your styles and scripts, it may misjudge the page or think it isn't mobile-friendly.
  3. Blocking pages that have a noindex tag. Google can't see the noindex if it can't crawl the page.
  4. Typos and wrong case. Paths are case-sensitive. /Blog and /blog are different.
  5. Putting the file in the wrong place. It must be at the root of the domain. A file at /files/robots.txt is ignored.

Blocking AI crawlers

Some AI companies use their own crawlers to collect training data, and they say they respect robots.txt. To opt out, add a group for each one:

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

User-agent: Google-Extended
Disallow: /

Google-Extended controls whether Google uses your content for its AI models. It doesn't affect normal Google Search crawling or rankings. Whether to block these is a business decision. Blocking may also keep your content out of some AI answers.

How to test it

  1. Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt in a browser. It should load as plain text.
  2. In Google Search Console, the robots.txt report shows the version Google last fetched and any errors.
  3. Run important pages through the Rankdesk SEO audit, which reads your robots.txt and tells you if the page is blocked and by which rule.

Create yours

The robots.txt and sitemap generator builds the file from your live site, keeps any rules you already have, lets you block private paths and AI crawlers with one setting, and adds your sitemap line. Upload it to your site's root folder, then test it.

On WordPress, plugins such as Yoast and Rank Math let you edit robots.txt from the dashboard. Shopify generates one automatically and lets you customise it through a template.

posts.title: XML Sitemaps: What to Include, What to Leave Out, and How to Submit
posts.seoTitle: XML Sitemaps: What to Include and How to Submit Them
posts.description: An XML sitemap lists the pages you want search engines to find. Learn what belongs in it, the limits, how to submit it and how to read the report.

toc.text: Tell search engines where it is

posts.html:
An XML sitemap is a file that lists the pages on your website you want search engines to know about. It's like handing Google a table of contents instead of making it find every page by following links.

Google can find pages without one, especially on small, well-linked sites. A sitemap still helps new pages get discovered sooner, makes sure deep pages aren't missed, and gives you a useful report in Search Console.

What a sitemap looks like

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <url>
    <loc>https://example.com/silk-sarees</loc>
    <lastmod>2026-10-01</lastmod>
  </url>
</urlset>

Each page is a <url> with its full address in <loc>. <lastmod> is the date the page content last changed.

You may see <changefreq> and <priority> in sitemaps too. Google has said it ignores both. It does use <lastmod> when the dates are consistently accurate, so only update it when the page really changes. Setting every page to today's date teaches Google to ignore the field.

What to include

Only pages you want in search results:

  • the page returns status 200
  • it isn't blocked by robots.txt
  • it has no noindex tag
  • it's the canonical version (not a duplicate pointing elsewhere with a canonical tag)

What to leave out

  • thank-you, cart, checkout and login pages
  • internal search results
  • filter and sort URLs such as ?color=red&sort=price
  • redirected URLs and pages that return 404
  • http:// versions if your site uses HTTPS
  • duplicate URLs with tracking parameters

A sitemap full of broken or duplicate URLs wastes crawling and makes the report harder to read.

Limits and sitemap indexes

One sitemap file can hold up to 50,000 URLs and be up to 50 MB uncompressed. Bigger sites split pages into several sitemaps and list them in a sitemap index:

<sitemapindex xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <sitemap><loc>https://example.com/sitemap-products.xml</loc></sitemap>
  <sitemap><loc>https://example.com/sitemap-blog.xml</loc></sitemap>
</sitemapindex>

Splitting by type (products, categories, blog) is also handy for small sites, because Search Console then reports indexing for each group separately.

How to create one

  • WordPress: Yoast, Rank Math and WordPress itself generate sitemaps automatically. Look for /sitemap_index.xml or /wp-sitemap.xml.
  • Shopify and Wix: created automatically at /sitemap.xml.
  • Custom or static sites: use the Rankdesk sitemap generator, which reads your live site's pages and builds the file. Upload it to your site's root folder.

Tell search engines where it is

  1. Add it to robots.txt: a line Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml lets every search engine find it.
  2. Submit it in Google Search Console: open Sitemaps, type the sitemap address and click Submit.
  3. Submit it in Bing Webmaster Tools too, which also feeds other search engines and assistants.

Reading the report

After submitting, Search Console shows whether the sitemap was read successfully and how many URLs it found. The Pages report (filtered by sitemap) then shows how many are indexed and why the rest aren't. Common reasons:

  • Discovered, currently not indexed: Google knows about the page but hasn't crawled it yet. Often a sign the site is new or the page looks low-value.
  • Crawled, currently not indexed: Google looked and chose not to index it. Improve the content or merge thin pages.
  • Duplicate without user-selected canonical: Google sees the page as a copy of another.
  • Excluded by noindex tag: expected for pages you hid on purpose, a problem if not.

A sitemap doesn't guarantee indexing. It tells Google what you'd like indexed. Quality and usefulness decide the rest.

A quick check

Run your home page through the SEO audit. It finds your sitemap through robots.txt, confirms it's valid, counts the URLs and checks whether the page you audited is listed.

posts.title: Local SEO Checklist for Shops and Service Businesses in India
posts.seoTitle: Local SEO Checklist for Shops and Service Businesses
posts.description: A practical checklist to rank in Google Maps and local results: Business Profile, website, reviews, citations and the mistakes to avoid.

toc.text: Mistakes that hold Indian businesses back

posts.html:
Local SEO is how a business shows up when people nearby search for what it offers, especially in the map results at the top of Google. For shops, clinics, restaurants, contractors and most service businesses, it matters more than any other kind of SEO.

Google says local rankings depend mainly on three things: relevance (how well your listing matches the search), distance (how close you are to the searcher or the place they named) and prominence (how well known and well reviewed you are). You can't move your shop, but you can improve the other two. Work through this list.

Google Business Profile

  • Profile claimed and verified. Follow our setup guide if not.
  • Business name exactly as on your signboard, no added keywords
  • Most specific primary category, plus relevant secondary categories
  • Map pin on your entrance
  • Phone number answered during business hours
  • Opening hours correct, including festival and holiday hours
  • Description that says what you do and where, written for customers
  • Every main product or service listed
  • At least 10 real photos: shopfront, inside, team, products or work
  • New photos and a post added every month
  • Questions on the profile answered

Reviews

  • A short review link saved and ready to send on WhatsApp
  • Every happy customer asked, at the moment they're happiest
  • Every review replied to, positive and negative
  • No paid, fake or incentivised reviews (see how to get reviews within the rules)

Your website

  • Name, address and phone in the footer of every page, as text, not an image
  • A contact page with an embedded Google map and directions from landmarks
  • Home page title tag with your main service and city
  • A separate page for each main service
  • If you serve several cities or areas, a genuinely useful page for each, with local details, not copy-pasted text with the city name swapped
  • LocalBusiness schema on the home or contact page
  • Click-to-call phone number and a WhatsApp button on mobile
  • Fast on mobile data. Many local searches happen on the go.

Citations and consistency

A citation is any mention of your business name, address and phone online.

  • Same name, address and phone everywhere: your website, Google, JustDial, IndiaMART, Sulekha, Facebook, Instagram and industry directories
  • Old addresses and numbers updated after a move
  • Duplicate listings removed or merged

Inconsistent details confuse search engines and customers. Our NAP consistency guide shows how to audit them.

Local reputation

  • Listed in your trade association and local chamber of commerce directories
  • Suppliers and partners link to your website
  • Mentions in local news, events or sponsorships
  • Local content on your website, such as projects in specific areas or guides for local customers

Language and search habits

  • Think about how local customers search. Many type in Hinglish ("saree shop near me surat") or their own language. See our guide to Hindi and Gujarati keywords.
  • Include landmarks and area names customers use, such as "near Iscon Cross Road" or "Ring Road market".

Mistakes that hold Indian businesses back

  1. Several listings for one shop, often created by staff or customers over the years.
  2. Keyword-stuffed names like "Best Dentist Vadodara Dental Clinic Painless". These risk suspension.
  3. A mobile number nobody answers. Missed calls become reviews like "never picks up".
  4. No website, or a website with no address. The profile and website support each other.
  5. Only asking family for reviews. Google filters reviews that look unnatural.

Measure it

In your Business Profile, check calls, direction requests and website clicks each month. In Search Console, look at searches that include your city or "near me". Rising numbers mean the checklist is working.

posts.title: Search Intent: Matching Pages to What People Actually Want
posts.description: Search intent is the reason behind a search. Learn the four types, how to spot them in Google's results and how to build the right page for each keyword.

toc.text: How to check intent for any keyword

posts.html:
Two searches can share the same words and want completely different things. "Silk saree" from someone ready to buy needs a product page with prices. "Silk saree care" needs a guide. Search intent is the reason behind a search, and matching it is one of the biggest factors in whether a page can rank at all.

If Google shows ten guides for a keyword, a product page won't break in, however well optimised it is. Google has learned what people want from that search, and it shows them that.

The four types of intent

Intent The searcher wants to Typical words Best page
Informational learn something how, what, why, guide, ideas Guide or blog post
Commercial compare options before buying best, top, vs, review, alternatives Comparison, review or list
Transactional buy, book or sign up buy, price, order, book, hire, quote Product, service or pricing page
Navigational reach a specific site brand names, "login" Your home or login page

Local searches ("near me", "in Ahmedabad") are usually transactional or commercial with a place attached. They need a page, and a Google Business Profile, that clearly serve that area.

How to check intent for any keyword

Don't guess. Search the keyword in Google, ideally in a private window, and look at the first page:

  1. What type of pages rank? Product pages, category pages, guides, videos, local map results?
  2. What format? Lists ("10 best…"), step-by-step guides, comparisons, calculators?
  3. What angle? Cheap, premium, for beginners, current year?
  4. What else does Google show? A map pack means local intent. Video results mean people want to watch. "People also ask" boxes show follow-up questions you should answer.

Whatever most of page one has in common is the intent you need to match.

Examples

  • "how to identify pure silk saree": informational. The results are guides and videos. Write a clear guide with the tests and photos, and link to your products at the end.
  • "best saree shop in surat": commercial and local. The results show the map pack and lists. Strengthen your Business Profile and reviews, and consider a page explaining what makes your shop different.
  • "banarasi silk saree price": transactional. The results are product and category pages with prices. Show prices or price ranges clearly.
  • "waterproofing vs tiling terrace": commercial. People are comparing. A fair comparison page with costs and pros and cons fits.

Mixed intent

Some searches have mixed results, say half guides and half product pages. That means people want different things. You can target it with the type that suits your business, or build a page that serves both, such as a category page with a short buying guide at the top.

Matching intent on the page

Once you know the intent, make it obvious from the first screen:

  • The title and H1 should promise what the searcher wants: "Banarasi Silk Sarees, Prices from ₹4,999" rather than "Our Collection".
  • The first paragraph should deliver it quickly. No long introductions before the answer.
  • The format should match: steps for how-to searches, a table for comparisons, prices and a buy button for transactional ones.
  • Next steps should follow naturally: a guide links to products, a product page links to care guides.

Intent explains traffic problems

If a page gets impressions in Search Console but few clicks, or clicks but people leave fast, check intent. A common cause is a page answering a different question from the one people searched. Rewriting the page to match is often more effective than any technical fix.

Plan by intent

When you use the keyword ideas tool, every idea is labelled local, commercial, buying or question. Group them by intent, then plan one page per group. It's the quickest way to make sure every page has a clear job. For the full process, see keyword research for beginners.

posts.title: Instagram Hashtags: How Many to Use and How to Choose Them
posts.description: Hashtags now work more like labels than a growth hack. Learn how many to use, how to mix niche, local and branded tags, and habits that limit reach.
posts.html:
A few years ago, the advice was to fill every caption with thirty hashtags. That era is over. Instagram has been cutting back how many hashtags it allows and says hashtags mainly help it understand what a post is about. Used well, they still help the right people find you. Used badly, they make posts look like spam.

What hashtags do today

Instagram uses many signals to decide who sees a post: your caption, what's in the image or video, the audio, and how people react. Hashtags are one of those signals. They label the topic, help a post appear on hashtag pages and in search, and group content such as customer photos under a branded tag.

They won't turn a weak post into a viral one. Content people save and share does that.

How many to use

Instagram has been reducing the maximum number of hashtags per post, and the exact limit has changed over time, so check what the app allows when you post. In practice, three to five well-chosen hashtags are enough for most businesses. Relevance matters far more than quantity.

The four kinds to mix

  1. Niche tags describe exactly what the post shows: #banarasisaree, #bathroomwaterproofing, #egglesscake. These reach people interested in that topic.
  2. Local tags reach people nearby: #suratfashion, #ahmedabadfood, #vadodarahomes. Essential for businesses that serve a city.
  3. Branded tags are yours alone: #shreetextiles. Customers can use them too, giving you a collection of real posts.
  4. Community tags reach a wider but related audience: #handloomlove, #madeinindia.

A good set for a saree post might be: #banarasisaree #silksaree #suratfashion #shreetextiles #handloomlove.

The Rankdesk hashtag generator builds these groups from your brand, keywords and city, so you can pick a balanced set quickly.

How to choose good tags

  • Search the tag first. Look at the top posts. If they don't match your content or audience, skip it.
  • Avoid huge generic tags like #love, #instagood or #fashion. Millions of posts bury yours instantly, and the audience isn't targeted.
  • Avoid very tiny tags that nobody uses or searches.
  • Check for banned or broken tags. Some tags get restricted because of spam. If a tag's page shows only a few top posts or a warning, don't use it.
  • Match the language your customers use. Hindi, Gujarati or Hinglish tags can reach local audiences with less competition.

Rotate your sets

Using exactly the same block of hashtags on every post can look automated. Keep three or four sets for your main content types (new arrivals, behind the scenes, customer photos, tips) and use the one that fits each post.

Where to put them

Hashtags in the caption or the first comment both work, but the caption is the safer choice because it's indexed with the post from the moment it goes live. Put them at the end of the caption, after the real text, so they don't distract readers.

Hashtags vs keywords

Instagram search now reads captions, names and bios too. A caption like "New Banarasi silk sarees for wedding season" already tells Instagram a lot. Hashtags work alongside keywords, not instead of them. Read our Instagram SEO guide for the full picture.

Habits that limit reach

  • Copying the same hashtags on every post for months
  • Hashtags unrelated to the post, added only because they're popular
  • Using engagement pods or follow-for-follow tags
  • Buying followers, which damages how Instagram rates your account

On Reels and YouTube

Reels follow the same rules: a few relevant hashtags plus keywords in the caption and on screen. On YouTube, hashtags in the description can appear above the title, but only the first few are shown and too many can cause YouTube to ignore them all. See our YouTube SEO guide.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals for Small Business Websites: LCP, INP and CLS
posts.seoTitle: Core Web Vitals for Small Business Sites: LCP, INP and CLS
posts.description: Core Web Vitals measure how fast, responsive and stable your pages feel. Learn what LCP, INP and CLS mean, the targets and the fixes that work.

toc.text: Fixing LCP: show the main content sooner
Fixing INP: make the page respond faster
Fixing CLS: stop the layout jumping

posts.html:
Core Web Vitals are three measurements Google uses to judge how a page feels to real visitors: how quickly the main content appears, how fast the page responds when you tap something, and whether the layout jumps around while loading. They're part of Google's page experience signals.

Their effect on rankings is real but modest. Great content on a slow page usually beats thin content on a fast one. But speed directly affects how many visitors stay, especially on mobile data, so it's worth getting right.

The three metrics

Metric Measures Good Poor
LCP, Largest Contentful Paint How long until the biggest image or text block appears 2.5 seconds or less Over 4 seconds
INP, Interaction to Next Paint How quickly the page reacts to taps, clicks and typing 200 ms or less Over 500 ms
CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift How much content moves unexpectedly while loading 0.1 or less Over 0.25

INP replaced an older metric, First Input Delay, in 2024. Google judges each metric at the 75th percentile of real visits, so most of your visitors need a good experience, not just the ones on fast phones.

Field data vs lab data

PageSpeed Insights shows two kinds of results:

  • Field data comes from real Chrome users over the last 28 days. This is what Google uses. Small sites may not have enough visitors to show it.
  • Lab data is a test run on a simulated phone. It's useful for finding problems, but the score can vary between runs.

Don't chase a perfect lab score of 100. Aim for good field data, or good lab metrics if there's no field data yet.

Fixing LCP: show the main content sooner

The largest element is usually a hero image, banner or slider.

  • Compress and resize images. A 4 MB photo from a phone camera is a common culprit. Convert to WebP or AVIF and serve the size actually displayed. Our image SEO guide covers this.
  • Don't lazy-load the hero image. Lazy loading is great below the fold, but it delays the main image. Add fetchpriority="high" to it instead.
  • Avoid sliders at the top of the page. They're heavy and rarely help conversions.
  • Improve server response. Cheap shared hosting can take over a second to respond. Caching plugins, a CDN or better hosting help.
  • Reduce render-blocking files. Too many CSS and JavaScript files in the head delay everything.

Fixing INP: make the page respond faster

Slow responses usually come from too much JavaScript:

  • Remove plugins and scripts you don't use, such as old chat widgets, sliders and tracking codes.
  • Load third-party scripts like chat, reviews and social feeds after the page is usable.
  • Choose lighter themes. Page builders that add lots of code can hurt INP.

Fixing CLS: stop the layout jumping

  • Set width and height on images and videos so the browser reserves space before they load.
  • Reserve space for ads, banners and embeds. Ads that push content down are a major cause of shift.
  • Load web fonts carefully. Use font-display: swap and similar fallback fonts so text doesn't jump.
  • Don't insert banners above existing content after the page loads, like cookie bars that push everything down.

WordPress quick wins

  1. Use a caching plugin.
  2. Install an image optimisation plugin that converts to WebP.
  3. Remove unused plugins.
  4. Choose a lightweight theme.
  5. Use a CDN, often included with good hosting.

Measure, fix, measure again

Run your key pages through the Rankdesk SEO audit, which includes Google's PageSpeed data for mobile or desktop with the biggest fixes listed. After changes, re-test. Field data in Search Console's Core Web Vitals report updates over the following four weeks, as new visits replace old ones.

posts.title: Canonical Tags: Fixing Duplicate Content Without Losing Rankings
posts.seoTitle: Canonical Tags: Fix Duplicate Content, Keep Rankings
posts.description: A canonical tag tells search engines which version of a page is the main one. Learn when you need it, how to write it and the mistakes to avoid.

toc.text: It's a hint, not a command

posts.html:
The same page can often be reached through several addresses. With and without www, with tracking codes from an ad, with a product filter applied, or through two different categories. To you it's one page. To a search engine, each address could be a separate page with identical content.

A canonical tag solves this by naming the main version. It tells Google: "If you find copies of this page, treat this address as the original."

What it looks like

It's a single line in the page's <head>:

<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/silk-sarees">

Every version of the page should carry the same canonical pointing to the preferred address. The preferred page should point to itself, called a self-referencing canonical, which is a good default for every page.

Why duplicates are a problem

Duplicate content isn't a penalty, but it causes real trouble:

  • Split signals. Links and attention spread across several URLs instead of building up one.
  • The wrong URL ranks. Google might show the version with a tracking code or the filtered view.
  • Wasted crawling. On large sites, crawlers spend time on copies instead of new pages.

Common sources of duplicates

  • http:// and https://, or www and non-www versions (fix these with redirects too)
  • trailing slashes: /page and /page/
  • tracking parameters: ?utm_source=whatsapp
  • filters and sorting: ?color=red&sort=price
  • the same product in two categories: /sarees/red-silk and /wedding/red-silk
  • printer-friendly or AMP versions
  • copies of your content on other sites (syndication)

Rules for canonical tags

  1. Use absolute URLs with https:// and your domain, not relative paths.
  2. Point to a page that works: status 200, not redirected, not noindex, not blocked by robots.txt.
  3. One canonical per page. Two conflicting tags, often added by a theme and a plugin, may both be ignored.
  4. Be consistent. Internal links, the sitemap and the canonical should all use the same preferred URL.
  5. Don't canonicalise different pages to one. Page 2 of a category isn't a duplicate of page 1. A blue saree page isn't a duplicate of the red one.

It's a hint, not a command

Google treats canonical tags as a strong suggestion. If other signals disagree, for example if all your internal links point to a different version, Google may choose its own canonical. Search Console's URL Inspection tool shows both the canonical you declared and the one Google selected.

Canonical vs redirect vs noindex

Situation Use
The page moved permanently A 301 redirect
Several URLs must keep working, such as filters or tracking links Canonical tag
A page should not appear in search at all noindex (see noindex vs robots.txt)

How to set it

  • WordPress: Yoast, Rank Math and similar plugins add self-referencing canonicals automatically and let you change them per page.
  • Shopify: canonicals are added automatically, including for products reached through collections.
  • Custom sites: add the tag to each page template. The meta tag generator includes it with your other head tags.

Check it

The Rankdesk SEO audit reports whether a page has a canonical tag and which URL it points to. Audit the versions people actually reach, such as a link with a tracking code, and make sure each one points to the clean URL.

posts.title: LocalBusiness Schema: The Fields That Matter for Shops and Service Businesses
posts.seoTitle: LocalBusiness Schema: The Fields That Matter
posts.description: LocalBusiness schema confirms your name, address, phone and hours to search engines. The fields worth filling, a full example and mistakes to avoid.

toc.text: The fields, in order of importance

posts.html:
If your business has a shop, office, clinic or service area, LocalBusiness schema is the structured data to add first. It states your key business facts in a format search engines read directly, and helps them connect your website with your Google Business Profile and listings elsewhere.

If schema is new to you, start with schema markup for beginners.

A complete example

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "ClothingStore",
  "name": "Shree Textiles",
  "url": "https://shreetextiles.in",
  "telephone": "+91-98765-43210",
  "image": "https://shreetextiles.in/images/shopfront.jpg",
  "priceRange": "₹₹",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "Plot 12, Ring Road Textile Market",
    "addressLocality": "Surat",
    "addressRegion": "Gujarat",
    "postalCode": "395002",
    "addressCountry": "IN"
  },
  "geo": {
    "@type": "GeoCoordinates",
    "latitude": 21.1950,
    "longitude": 72.8406
  },
  "openingHours": "Mo-Sa 10:00-19:00",
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.instagram.com/shreetextiles",
    "https://www.facebook.com/shreetextiles"
  ]
}

Wrap it in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag on your home page or contact page.

The fields, in order of importance

Required in practice

  • @type: use the most specific type that fits, such as Dentist, Restaurant, ClothingStore, Plumber, HomeAndConstructionBusiness, AccountingService or Bakery. All of them are kinds of LocalBusiness, so they accept the same fields.
  • name: exactly as on your signboard and Google Business Profile.
  • address: street, city, state, PIN code and country code IN. Match the format you use everywhere else.

Strongly recommended

  • telephone: with the country code, +91.
  • url: your website's main address.
  • openingHours or the more detailed openingHoursSpecification for different hours on different days.
  • geo: latitude and longitude. Right-click your entrance in Google Maps to copy them.
  • image: a real photo of the business, such as the shopfront.

Useful extras

  • priceRange: a rough guide like ₹₹ or ₹500–₹5,000.
  • sameAs: links to your official social profiles and listings. This helps confirm all of them are the same business.
  • areaServed: cities or regions, for businesses that travel to customers.
  • logo, email and aggregateRating (only if real reviews appear on the page itself).

Several branches

Each branch should have its own page on your website, such as /branches/vadodara, with its own LocalBusiness schema, address, phone and hours. Don't put several addresses in one block on the home page.

Service-area businesses

If customers don't visit you, for example a pest control or painting service, you can leave out the street address and use areaServed instead:

"areaServed": ["Ahmedabad", "Gandhinagar"]

Keep this consistent with your Google Business Profile, where you can also hide the address and show a service area.

Mistakes to avoid

  1. Details that don't match the page or your Google profile. If the footer shows one phone number and the schema another, you weaken trust in both.
  2. Ratings that aren't on the page. Google's rules say review markup must reflect reviews visible to visitors. Don't copy your Google rating into schema without showing reviews on the page.
  3. Keywords in the name. "name": "Shree Textiles Best Saree Shop Surat" breaks the same rules as keyword-stuffed Business Profile names.
  4. Duplicate blocks. Many themes and plugins add their own schema. Check for duplicates before adding more.
  5. Wrong page. The business block belongs on pages about the business, not on every blog post.

Build and test it

The Rankdesk schema generator has a local business type with every field above. Enter your website and it pulls your name, phone, address, social links and existing schema automatically. Then test the page with Google's Rich Results Test and fix any warnings.

Local schema works best together with a complete Google Business Profile and consistent details across the web.

posts.title: H1, H2, H3: How to Structure Headings for SEO and Readers
posts.description: Headings give a page its outline for readers, screen readers and search engines. Use one H1, nest H2s and H3s properly and fix theme mistakes.
posts.html:
Headings are the outline of a page. Readers skim them to decide whether to stay. Screen readers use them to jump between sections. Search engines use them to understand what each part of the page covers. Good headings help all three.

The levels

HTML has six heading levels, <h1> to <h6>. Most pages only need three:

  • H1: the title of the page. What the whole page is about.
  • H2: the main sections.
  • H3: sub-sections inside an H2.

Think of a book: H1 is the book title, H2s are chapters, H3s are sections within chapters.

H1 Bathroom Waterproofing in Ahmedabad
  H2 Signs your bathroom needs waterproofing
  H2 Our waterproofing methods
    H3 Chemical coating
    H3 Membrane waterproofing
  H2 Prices
  H2 Frequently asked questions

One H1 per page

Use one H1 that clearly states the page's topic, usually close to your title tag. Google has said it can handle pages with several H1s, but one clear H1 makes the structure obvious to everyone and avoids confusion about what the page is mainly about.

Common problems:

  • No H1 at all. Some themes style the page title with a <div> or <p>.
  • The logo as the H1 on every page, so every page has the same main heading.
  • Several H1s because a page builder uses H1 for every big piece of text.

Don't skip levels

Go down one level at a time: H1, then H2, then H3. Jumping from H1 straight to H4 because you like the H4 font size breaks the outline. Choose the heading level for the structure, then style it with CSS to look however you want.

Write useful headings

  • Make them descriptive. "Prices" or "How much does waterproofing cost?" tells the reader what's below. "Section 2" or "More info" doesn't.
  • Use your keywords naturally. H2s are a good place for related search phrases, such as "terrace waterproofing cost". Don't force the same phrase into every heading.
  • Questions work well. Headings that match questions people ask can help your page appear for those searches.
  • Keep them short. A heading is a signpost, not a paragraph.

Headings aren't for styling

Don't use a heading tag just to make text big or bold, like a phone number, a slogan or a "Call now!" banner. Use normal text and style it. Headings should only mark sections.

The reverse is also a problem: section titles that are only bold paragraphs. They look like headings but don't work as headings for screen readers or search engines.

Checking headings in your theme

Themes often use heading tags in places you wouldn't expect: the site name in the header, widget titles in the sidebar ("Recent posts"), and footer column titles. These aren't always wrong, but they add noise to the outline.

The Rankdesk SEO audit shows a page's full heading outline, flags missing or multiple H1s and points to any skipped levels. Run it on a few page types (home, product, blog post) because each template can have different problems.

Headings and featured snippets

Clear structure helps Google pull answers from your page. A heading phrased as a question, followed directly by a short, clear answer, and then more detail, is the format most likely to be used for a featured snippet or a "People also ask" answer.

Quick checklist

  • One H1 that describes the page
  • H2s for main sections, H3s inside them, no skipped levels
  • Descriptive headings that use natural keywords
  • No headings used only for styling
  • Section titles marked up as real headings

posts.title: Open Graph Tags: Make Your Links Look Good on WhatsApp and LinkedIn
posts.seoTitle: Open Graph Tags: Better WhatsApp and LinkedIn Previews
posts.description: Open Graph tags control the title, description and image when your link is shared. The essential tags, the right image size and how to refresh a preview.

toc.text: Fixing a preview that won't update

posts.html:
When you share a link on WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn or X, the app shows a preview card with a title, short description and image. That card comes from Open Graph tags in your page's code. Without them, apps guess, and the result is often a cropped logo, the wrong text or no image at all.

For many Indian businesses, WhatsApp is where links get shared most. A good preview makes people far more likely to tap.

The essential tags

<meta property="og:title" content="Pure Silk Sarees from Surat">
<meta property="og:description" content="Banarasi and Kanjivaram sarees direct from our looms. Delivery across India.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://shreetextiles.in/og/silk-sarees.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://shreetextiles.in/silk-sarees">
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="Shree Textiles">
  • og:title: the headline on the card. It can be the same as your title tag, often without the brand suffix.
  • og:description: one or two sentences. Many apps show only the first line, so lead with the important part.
  • og:image: the full https:// address of the image. Relative paths like /og.jpg often fail.
  • og:url: the page's preferred address, usually the same as its canonical tag.
  • og:type: website for most pages, article for blog posts, product for products.

Twitter (X) cards

X reads Open Graph tags as a fallback, but add this one for a large image card:

<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

The image matters most

  • Size: 1200 × 630 pixels works across WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn and X.
  • File: JPG or PNG, kept small, ideally well under 1 MB. Very large images may not show in WhatsApp.
  • Safe area: keep text and logos away from the edges, as some apps crop the image to a square.
  • Content: a clear photo of the product or your work, or a simple branded graphic with the page title. Avoid small text that's unreadable on phones.
  • One per page where you can. A unique image for each product or blog post looks better than one logo everywhere.

Fixing a preview that won't update

Apps save previews, so changing your tags doesn't update links already shared. To refresh:

  • Facebook and Instagram: paste the URL into Facebook's Sharing Debugger and click "Scrape again".
  • LinkedIn: use the Post Inspector.
  • WhatsApp: it caches previews too. Sharing the URL with a small change, such as adding ?v=2, usually forces a fresh preview.

Common mistakes

  1. No og:image, so apps pick a random image or none.
  2. A logo as the image, cropped badly in square previews.
  3. The same title and image on every page.
  4. Blocking the image with robots.txt or a login, so apps can't fetch it.
  5. Tags added by JavaScript after the page loads. Most apps read the raw HTML and don't run scripts.

WordPress and builders

Yoast and Rank Math have a "Social" tab on each page where you set the image and text. Shopify themes use the product image by default. Wix and Squarespace have social share settings per page.

Create and preview them

The Rankdesk meta tag generator writes all of these tags together with your title and description, and shows a live preview of the share card. The SEO audit checks which Open Graph tags a page is missing.

posts.title: Long-Tail Keywords: Why Small Sites Should Start Here
posts.description: Long-tail keywords are longer, specific searches with fewer competitors and clearer intent. Learn why they suit new websites and how to find and target them.

toc.text: Why they suit new and small sites
How to target them without creating thin pages

posts.html:
"Saree" is a huge search. Thousands of websites compete for it, including marketplaces with enormous budgets. "Banarasi silk saree for wedding under 10000" is searched far less, but by someone who knows exactly what they want. That second kind of search is a long-tail keyword, and it's where small websites win.

What makes a keyword long-tail

The name comes from a chart of searches: a few very popular terms at the "head", followed by a long "tail" of millions of specific searches each made less often. Together, the tail accounts for a large share of all searches.

Long-tail keywords are usually:

  • Longer, often three words or more
  • More specific about product, place, budget, problem or audience
  • Less competitive, because fewer pages target them
  • Clearer in intent, so it's easier to build exactly the right page

Length isn't the real test. "Waterproofing contractor Bopal" is long-tail because it's specific, even though it's only three words.

Why they suit new and small sites

  1. You can rank sooner. Big brands rarely build pages for narrow searches.
  2. The traffic converts. Someone searching "dentist in Vadodara open Sunday" is ready to book.
  3. They add up. Twenty pages each bringing 30 targeted visitors beat one page stuck on page five for a broad term.
  4. They build toward the head. As your site gains authority from many specific pages, broader terms become reachable.

Kinds of long-tail keywords

  • Product plus detail: "pure silk saree with silver zari"
  • Product plus place: "saree wholesale market Surat"
  • Product plus price or budget: "kitchen sink under 5000"
  • Problem-based: "bathroom wall damp after rain"
  • Questions: "how long does waterproofing last"
  • Audience: "accounting software for small shops"
  • Comparison: "membrane vs chemical waterproofing"

How to find them

  • Google autocomplete: type your main keyword and add each letter of the alphabet after it.
  • People also ask and related searches on the results page.
  • Your customers' words: WhatsApp chats, emails and phone calls are full of real long-tail searches.
  • Search Console: the Performance report lists long searches you already appear for, often on page two. These are your quickest wins.
  • The keyword ideas tool: expands each seed into local, buying, comparison and question versions.

How to target them without creating thin pages

A common mistake is building a separate page for every small variation. "Silk saree price", "silk saree rate" and "silk saree cost" mean the same thing and belong on one page.

Group long-tail keywords by intent:

  • If they want the same thing, cover them on one page, using the variations in headings and text.
  • If they want different things, give them separate pages.

Questions often fit best as sections of a larger guide or in an FAQ at the bottom of a service page.

Writing for a long-tail keyword

  • Put the phrase, or a natural version of it, in the title tag, the H1 and the opening paragraph.
  • Answer the specific question quickly. Someone searching "how long does waterproofing last" wants a number early, followed by the detail.
  • Add the details the search implies: prices for "under 10000", areas and directions for local searches, steps for "how to".
  • Link to your related product or service pages so readers can act.

A simple plan

  1. Pick your main product or service.
  2. Collect 30 to 50 long-tail variations.
  3. Group them by intent into 5 to 10 page ideas.
  4. Improve existing pages first, then write the missing ones, one a week.
  5. After a few months, check Search Console for new long-tail searches you appear for, and repeat.

For the whole process from the beginning, read keyword research for beginners.

posts.title: YouTube SEO: Titles, Descriptions, Tags and Chapters
posts.description: YouTube is a search engine too. Learn how to research topics, write titles and descriptions, add chapters and captions, and use tags so your videos get found.
posts.html:
YouTube is one of the most used search engines in India. People search it for product reviews, how-to guides, recipes and demonstrations before they buy. Videos also appear in Google results, often near the top for "how to" searches. Optimising a video takes a few extra minutes and helps it keep getting views long after you post it.

Start with what people search

Before filming, check what people actually look for:

  • Type your topic into YouTube's search bar and note the autocomplete suggestions.
  • Look at the top results. Their titles, lengths and thumbnails show what viewers expect.
  • Check Google for "how to" searches on the topic. If Google shows video results, it's a good video topic.
