Pick one clear topic per video, matching a real search such as "how to drape a silk saree" or "terrace waterproofing process".

Titles

The title is the strongest text signal and the main reason people click.

  • Put the main search phrase near the start: "How to Drape a Silk Saree in 5 Minutes (Easy Steps)".
  • Keep the important part under about 60 characters, as longer titles get cut on phones.
  • Promise something specific and deliver it. Misleading titles get clicks but lose viewers fast, which hurts the video.

Descriptions

  • The first two lines show in search and above the "more" link. Use them to describe the video with your main keyword naturally.
  • Below that, write a fuller summary of what the video covers, a few paragraphs in plain language.
  • Add links to your website, products and related videos.
  • Include contact details or your shop address if you serve customers locally.

Chapters

Chapters split a video into labelled sections, making it easier to watch and helping Google show "key moments" in search. Add timestamps in the description:

00:00 Introduction
00:45 Pleating the saree
02:10 Draping the pallu
03:30 Pinning tips

YouTube's rules: the first timestamp must be 00:00, you need at least three, and each chapter must be at least 10 seconds long.

Captions

Upload accurate captions or correct YouTube's automatic ones. Captions help viewers watching without sound and people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and they give YouTube an accurate transcript of your words. If you film in Hindi or Gujarati, add captions in that language, and an English version if your audience is mixed.

Say your keywords

YouTube can understand what's spoken. Saying "in this video I'll show how to drape a silk saree" early on reinforces the topic.

Tags and hashtags

Tags play a small role. YouTube says they mainly help with common misspellings. Add a few: your main phrase, common variations and your brand. The hashtag generator creates a YouTube tag list within the 500-character limit.

Hashtags in the description can show above the title. Use a few relevant ones. Adding too many can make YouTube ignore all of them.

Thumbnails

A clear custom thumbnail affects clicks more than almost anything else: a close-up of the result, a face showing emotion, or a few large words. Make sure it's readable at phone size.

Keep people watching

YouTube rewards videos people watch and enjoy. Get to the point in the first 15 seconds, cut long pauses, show rather than tell, and end with a link to a related video or playlist.

Playlists

Group related videos into playlists with keyword-rich titles, such as "Saree Draping Styles". Playlists can rank on their own and keep viewers watching more of your videos.

Use video on your website

Embed relevant videos on your website pages, such as a product video on its product page. It helps visitors and can make your page eligible for video results in Google. For more on social search, read our Instagram SEO guide.

posts.title: How to Get More Google Reviews (Without Breaking the Rules)
posts.description: Reviews affect your local ranking and whether people choose you. The allowed ways to ask, practices that get reviews removed, and how to reply.
posts.html:
Reviews do two jobs. They're one of the signals Google uses for local rankings, and they're what people read before they call you instead of the shop down the road. Most happy customers never think to leave one. The difference between businesses with 10 reviews and 200 is usually just asking, consistently.

Get your review link

  1. Open your Google Business Profile while signed in.
  2. Look for Ask for reviews or Get more reviews.
  3. Copy the short link. When customers open it, the review box appears directly.

Save it somewhere handy, such as a WhatsApp quick reply, your email signature and a QR code at the counter.

When to ask

Ask at the moment the customer is happiest:

  • right after a successful delivery or installation
  • when a customer thanks you or says they're happy
  • after a problem was solved well
  • when a project is handed over

A message sent the same day gets far more reviews than one sent a week later.

How to ask

Keep it personal and short:

Thank you for choosing us for your bathroom waterproofing, Mr. Patel! If you're happy with the work, would you share a quick Google review? It helps other families find us: [link]

Some ideas that work:

  • Train your team to ask in person, then send the link on WhatsApp.
  • Put a QR code on bills, packaging, the counter and visiting cards.
  • Mention what to write about, such as the product, service or staff member, so reviews are more useful to others. Don't tell them what rating to give.

What's not allowed

Google's rules are strict, and breaking them can get reviews removed or your profile restricted:

  • No paying or rewarding for reviews, including discounts, gifts or contest entries.
  • No review gating: you can't ask only happy customers, or filter people through a "were you satisfied?" step that sends only the happy ones to Google. You can ask everyone.
  • No fake reviews, including reviews written by staff, family or friends posing as customers, or bought from review sellers.
  • No reviewing competitors or asking others to.
  • No reviews from your own premises in bulk, such as handing customers a shop tablet. Many reviews from one device or network can be filtered.

Google uses automated systems to detect patterns, and suspicious reviews often disappear.

Replying to reviews

Reply to every review. It shows you care, and future customers read the replies as much as the reviews.

Positive reviews: thank the person by name, mention something specific and keep it short.

Thank you, Riya! We're glad the Banarasi saree was perfect for your sister's wedding. See you next season!

Negative reviews: stay calm and professional. Others will judge you by how you respond.

  1. Thank them for the feedback.
  2. Apologise for the experience, without arguing details in public.
  3. Explain briefly what you've done or will do.
  4. Offer to continue privately with a phone number or email.

We're sorry the delivery was late, Mr. Shah. That isn't the standard we aim for. We've changed our dispatch process to stop it happening again. Please call us on 98765 43210 so we can make this right.

Fake or abusive reviews

If a review breaks Google's policies, for example spam, hate speech, a conflict of interest or a review meant for another business, report it from your Business Profile. Google decides whether to remove it. A review being negative isn't by itself a reason for removal.

Show reviews on your website

You can display Google reviews on your site with an embed or by quoting them. If you add review schema, the reviews must be visible on that page, and Google doesn't show star ratings in results for a business's reviews of itself on its own website.

Reviews are one part of the local SEO checklist. Combined with a complete Business Profile, they make a strong difference in the map results.

posts.title: 301 vs 302 Redirects: Which One to Use and When
posts.description: Redirects send visitors and search engines from an old URL to a new one. The difference between 301 and 302, when to use each and how to avoid chains.
posts.html:
A redirect sends anyone who visits one URL to another URL automatically. You need them whenever a page moves: a new website, a renamed product, a switch to HTTPS or merged pages. Done right, visitors and search engines barely notice. Done wrong, you lose traffic and rankings you spent years building.

The two you'll use

Code Meaning Use when
301 Moved permanently The old URL is gone for good
302 Found (moved temporarily) The old URL will come back

There are also 308 (permanent) and 307 (temporary). They behave like 301 and 302 but guarantee the request method stays the same, which matters for forms and APIs more than ordinary pages. Google treats 308 like 301 and 307 like 302.

What Google does with each

Google has said both permanent and temporary redirects pass ranking signals. The difference is which URL Google keeps in its results:

  • With a 301, Google understands the new URL is the one to show and moves its attention there.
  • With a 302, Google may keep showing the old URL for a while, expecting it to return.

So use 301 for permanent changes. If a 302 stays in place for a long time, Google may eventually treat it as permanent anyway, but there's no reason to rely on that.

When to use a 301

  • moving from http:// to https://
  • choosing www or non-www and redirecting the other
  • changing your domain name
  • renaming a page's URL, such as /product-12 to /red-silk-saree
  • merging two thin pages into one stronger page
  • deleting a page that has a close replacement

When to use a 302

  • a product temporarily out of stock that redirects to its category
  • a seasonal page sending visitors to a temporary offer
  • testing a new page before switching permanently
  • sending visitors to a maintenance page during short downtime

Redirect chains and loops

A chain is when URL A redirects to B, which redirects to C. Each hop slows the page and adds a chance for something to break. Search engines follow several hops, but not forever. After a site moves twice, old links often go through chains without anyone noticing.

Fix chains by pointing every old URL straight to the final destination, and update your internal links to the final URL so no redirect is needed at all.

A loop is when URLs redirect to each other forever (A to B, B to A). Browsers show an error like "too many redirects" and the page can't be reached.

Deleted pages: redirect or 404?

Redirect a deleted page only when there's a genuinely relevant replacement. Redirecting everything to the home page confuses visitors, and Google often treats those as "soft 404s" anyway. If there's no replacement, let the page return 404 or 410 (gone). That's a normal part of a website changing.

Moving a whole website

  1. List every important old URL, using your sitemap, Search Console and analytics.
  2. Map each one to its new URL in a spreadsheet.
  3. Set up 301 redirects for every row, one to one.
  4. Update internal links, canonical tags and the sitemap to the new URLs.
  5. For a domain change, use Search Console's Change of Address tool.
  6. Keep the redirects in place for at least a year, ideally permanently.
  7. Watch Search Console for errors in the following weeks.

How to set up redirects

  • WordPress: a redirect plugin such as Redirection, or the redirect manager in your SEO plugin.
  • Shopify: Online Store, Navigation, URL Redirects. Shopify can also create them automatically when you change a product URL.
  • Apache hosting: rules in the .htaccess file.
  • Vercel, Netlify and similar: a redirects setting in the project configuration.

Check your redirects

The Rankdesk SEO audit shows the full redirect chain for any URL, flags temporary redirects that should be permanent and warns about multiple hops. Audit your old URLs after any move to confirm each one lands on the right page in one step. Moving to HTTPS? Read HTTPS and SEO too.

posts.title: FAQ Schema: When It Still Helps and When to Skip It
posts.description: Google now shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health sites. What that means for your site and when FAQ markup still helps.

toc.text: Does that make FAQ schema useless?
Why a visible FAQ section still helps
When to add FAQ schema now

posts.html:
For a few years, FAQ schema was one of the easiest ways to make a search result bigger. Add questions and answers in structured data, and Google might show them as expandable drop-downs under your link. Many websites added FAQ markup to every page for this reason.

That changed in 2023, and plenty of sites still haven't caught up.

What changed

In August 2023, Google announced it would show FAQ rich results only for well-known, authoritative government and health websites. For other sites, FAQ drop-downs no longer appear in normal search results, even with valid markup. At the same time, Google stopped showing HowTo rich results.

So if you run a shop, agency, blog or service business, adding FAQ schema won't bring back the expanded result.

Does that make FAQ schema useless?

Not entirely, but its value is now much smaller:

  • It doesn't hurt. Google said there's no need to remove existing FAQ markup, and valid markup causes no problems.
  • It labels content clearly. Structured question-and-answer pairs are easy for any system to understand, including other search engines and AI tools.
  • It's not a ranking boost. It never was.

The bigger value was always in the visible FAQ section itself, and that hasn't changed.

Why a visible FAQ section still helps

A good FAQ section on a service or product page:

  • answers the questions that stop people buying, such as price, time, warranty and delivery
  • matches the long-tail questions people search, such as "how long does waterproofing last"
  • can be used by Google for "People also ask" answers or featured snippets, which don't need FAQ schema
  • reduces calls and messages asking the same things

When to add FAQ schema now

Add it if:

  • the page has a real FAQ section visible to visitors
  • the questions and answers are written by you, not by users (user questions with several answers suit QAPage instead)
  • you can add it easily, for example through your SEO plugin or a generator

Skip it, or don't prioritise it, if:

  • you'd be adding questions only for the markup, without showing them on the page
  • you'd need to hire a developer just for this
  • you have more valuable markup to add first, such as LocalBusiness or Product

The rules still apply

If you use FAQ schema, follow Google's guidelines:

  1. Every question and answer in the markup must be visible on the page.
  2. Don't use it for advertising, such as "Why are we the best?" with a sales pitch.
  3. Each question should appear once on the site, rather than the same FAQ copied onto every page.
  4. Answers can include links and simple formatting, but keep them accurate.

Example

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "FAQPage",
  "mainEntity": [{
    "@type": "Question",
    "name": "How long does terrace waterproofing last?",
    "acceptedAnswer": {
      "@type": "Answer",
      "text": "A properly applied membrane system usually lasts 8 to 10 years. We give a 5-year written warranty."
    }
  }]
}

Writing good FAQ answers

  • Start with the direct answer, then explain.
  • Keep each answer to two to four sentences where possible.
  • Use the words customers use, from phone calls, WhatsApp and reviews.
  • Update answers when prices, policies or processes change.

The Rankdesk schema generator can build FAQ markup from questions already on your page. For an overview of which schema types matter most now, read schema markup for beginners.

posts.title: Internal Linking for Small Sites: A Practical Plan
posts.description: Internal links help visitors find more and help search engines discover your pages. A simple plan for menus, in-text links and anchor text.

toc.text: A plan for a small site

posts.html:
Internal links are links from one page on your website to another page on the same website. They're easy to overlook, but they do three important jobs:

  1. Help visitors find related information and the next step, such as from a guide to a product.
  2. Help search engines discover pages. Crawlers find most pages by following links. A page with no internal links pointing to it, an "orphan page", may never be found.
  3. Show what matters. Pages that many others link to look important. The words in a link tell search engines what the target page is about.

Types of internal links

  • Navigation: the main menu, header and footer. Every page gets these, so use them for your most important pages.
  • Breadcrumbs: "Home / Sarees / Banarasi" at the top of a page. They show structure and give easy links back up.
  • Contextual links: links inside the text of a page. These are the most useful for both readers and search engines, because the surrounding text explains the connection.
  • Related content: "You might also like" sections at the end of posts or products.

Anchor text

The anchor text is the clickable words. It should describe the page it links to:

  • Good: "see our guide to canonical tags"
  • Weak: "to learn more, click here"

Descriptive anchors help screen reader users too, as they often jump from link to link. Vary the wording naturally. You don't need the exact keyword every time.

A plan for a small site

1. Decide your most important pages

Usually your home page, main service or product category pages and contact page. These should be in the main menu and get the most links.

2. Link down from categories, up from details

A category page links to each product or service in it. Each product or service page links back to its category and to closely related items.

3. Connect guides to money pages

Every blog post or guide should link to at least one relevant service or product page, where it genuinely helps the reader. A guide on "how to identify pure silk" naturally links to your silk saree collection.

4. Link new pages from old ones

When you publish something new, find two or three existing pages on related topics and add a link to the new page. This gets it discovered faster than waiting for the sitemap.

5. Fix orphan pages

Check your sitemap against your menus and content. Any page in the sitemap that nothing links to needs at least one link, or should be removed if it isn't useful.

How many links per page?

There's no fixed number. Add links where they help the reader. A long guide might have ten contextual links, while a short product page might have three. What to avoid is a block of dozens of links that serve no reader, such as a footer listing every city you've ever served.

Common mistakes

  • Links only in the menu, with none inside the content.
  • Broken internal links after renaming or deleting pages. Update links rather than relying on redirects.
  • Linking to redirected URLs such as http:// versions or old addresses.
  • Using images as links without alt text, which leaves the link with no description.
  • Using nofollow on internal links. It's rarely needed and can stop crawlers following paths you want found.

Check your links

The Rankdesk SEO audit counts the internal and external links on a page and flags links with no readable text. For a whole-site view, the free version of Screaming Frog crawls up to 500 URLs and shows pages with few links pointing to them. Our free SEO tools list has more options.

posts.title: Hindi, Gujarati and Hinglish Keywords: Reaching Searchers in Their Language
posts.seoTitle: Hindi, Gujarati and Hinglish Keywords for Local SEO
posts.description: Many Indian customers search in Hindi, Gujarati or a Roman-script mix. How these searches differ, how to find them and how to build pages for them.

toc.text: Local language on Google Business Profile
Local language on Instagram and YouTube

posts.html:
Not every customer types "silk saree shop near me". Some type "सिल्क साड़ी", some type "silk saree ni dukan", and many type a mix of English and Hindi in Roman letters, like "sasti saree kaha milegi". Voice search adds even more variety. If your website only speaks formal English, you may be invisible to a large share of your local market.

Three kinds of local-language searches

  1. Native script: Hindi in Devanagari (साड़ी), Gujarati in Gujarati script (સાડી). Common on phones with local-language keyboards and with voice search.
  2. Transliterated (Hinglish or Gujlish): local words in Roman letters, such as "saree kitne ki hai", "ghar banavva mate contractor".
  3. Mixed: English product words with local grammar, such as "wedding saree under 5000 surat mein".

Google treats each as a different search with its own results. That's an opportunity, because far fewer websites target them.

How to find them

  • Listen to customers. How do they phrase things on WhatsApp and phone calls? That's your keyword list.
  • Google autocomplete works in every language. Type in Hindi or Gujarati script, or in Hinglish, and note the suggestions.
  • Google Keyword Planner lets you choose the language, including Hindi and Gujarati, and location, to see volume for native-script terms.
  • Google Trends can compare an English term with its Hindi or Hinglish version in a specific state.
  • YouTube search shows how people search for videos, which is often in the local language.
  • Search Console: look at the searches your site already appears for. You may find Hinglish searches you never targeted.

The keyword ideas tool accepts seed keywords in any language or script, so you can expand Hinglish seeds the same way as English ones.

Should you translate your website?

It depends on your customers.

  • If most of your customers prefer a local language, create proper translated pages: a Hindi or Gujarati version of your important pages, written by a fluent person, not machine translation left unchecked.
  • If your customers are mixed, keep English as the main language, and add local-language sections where they help, such as an FAQ in Gujarati or a Hindi summary on service pages.
  • For Hinglish searches, you don't need a separate language version. Use the common phrases naturally in headings, FAQs and descriptions where they fit.

Doing multilingual pages properly

If you create separate language versions:

  1. Give each its own URL, such as /hi/ and /gu/ folders. Don't switch languages on the same URL with a button, because search engines will only see one version.
  2. Set the language in the HTML, such as <html lang="hi"> or <html lang="gu">.
  3. Add hreflang tags linking each version to the others, so Google shows the right one to each searcher:
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-IN" href="https://example.com/sarees">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="hi-IN" href="https://example.com/hi/sarees">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="gu-IN" href="https://example.com/gu/sarees">
  1. Translate the meta tags too: the title tag, meta description and image alt text.
  2. Let people switch with a visible language link, never an automatic redirect based on location.

Local language on Google Business Profile

Your Business Profile is in one language, but customer reviews come in many. Reply in the language the customer used. It's friendlier, and the words in reviews and replies add local-language context to your listing.

Local language on Instagram and YouTube

Social search is where local-language content does especially well. Reels and videos in Hindi or Gujarati with matching captions, hashtags and on-screen text can reach audiences English content misses. See our guides to Instagram SEO and YouTube SEO.

Write naturally

Whatever the language, write for the reader. Forcing awkward phrases like "saree kaha milega surat best shop" into sentences reads badly in any language. Use local-language terms where your customers would expect them, and let the content do the rest.

posts.title: NAP Consistency: Why Your Name, Address and Phone Must Match Everywhere
posts.seoTitle: NAP Consistency: Match Name, Address and Phone Everywhere
posts.description: NAP means name, address and phone. Mismatched details across your website, Google profile and directories confuse search engines. Find and fix them.

toc.text: Step 4: Make your website the reference

posts.html:
NAP stands for Name, Address and Phone number, the three details that identify a local business online. Every place your business is listed, from your website and Google Business Profile to JustDial, IndiaMART, Facebook and trade directories, should show them the same way.

It sounds minor, but inconsistent details are one of the most common problems we find when auditing local businesses.

Why it matters

For search engines: Google builds a picture of your business from many sources. When your website, profile and directories agree, Google is more confident in the details, which supports your local rankings. When they conflict, such as an old address on one site and a different phone number on another, that confidence drops.

For customers: an old number that doesn't connect or an address you moved from three years ago means a lost customer, and often an angry review.

Where inconsistencies come from

  • moving premises and updating only some listings
  • changing phone numbers, or using a staff member's personal number
  • listings created by customers, data aggregators or former employees
  • different name formats: "Shree Textiles", "Shri Textiles", "Shree Textiles Pvt Ltd", "Shree Textile Surat"
  • address variations: "Ring Road" vs "Ring Rd", missing PIN codes, different landmarks
  • duplicate listings on the same directory

Small formatting differences like "Rd" vs "Road" are usually understood. The serious problems are wrong or outdated details, different names and duplicates.

Step 1: Decide your official NAP

Write down one version and use it everywhere:

  • Name: exactly as on your signboard and legal registration, without extra keywords.
  • Address: one consistent format, including shop number, building, street, area, city, state and PIN code.
  • Phone: one main number, ideally a landline or a dedicated business mobile, with +91 where the format allows.

Step 2: Find your listings

Search Google for:

  • your business name
  • your phone number in quotes, including old numbers
  • your old addresses, if you've moved

Then check the directories common in your industry: JustDial, Sulekha, IndiaMART, TradeIndia, Yellow Pages India, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, Zomato or Practo if relevant, and your trade association directory. Note each listing and what it shows in a spreadsheet.

Step 3: Fix and merge

  • Update every listing you control to the official NAP.
  • Claim listings you don't control yet, then update them.
  • Ask directories to merge or remove duplicate listings. Most have a "report incorrect information" or support option.
  • For Google, suggest edits to wrong details on Maps and mark duplicate profiles for removal.

Step 4: Make your website the reference

Your website should be the clearest source of your details:

  • NAP in the footer of every page, as real text (not inside an image).
  • A contact page with the full address, phone, map and opening hours.
  • LocalBusiness schema with exactly the same name, address and phone.
  • Click-to-call phone links on mobile.

The schema generator pulls your name, phone and address from your website, which is a quick way to spot whether your own pages are consistent.

Step 5: Keep it consistent

Whenever something changes, update every listing in your spreadsheet the same week. Check once or twice a year for new listings created by others. Many businesses fix their NAP once, then a new branch or phone number undoes it.

Several locations

Each location needs its own consistent NAP, its own Google Business Profile, and its own page on your website. Don't use one central phone number for every branch on Google if each branch has its own line.

NAP consistency is one item in our local SEO checklist. It isn't glamorous, but it removes a quiet drag on local rankings.

posts.title: Image SEO: Alt Text, File Names, WebP and Lazy Loading
posts.description: Images can bring search traffic or slow your site down. Learn how to write alt text, name files, choose formats and sizes, and load images so pages stay fast.

toc.text: 6. Lazy-load below the fold, not above

posts.html:
Images do a lot of work on a business website: they show products, prove the quality of your work and make pages worth reading. They can also be the main reason a page is slow. Good image SEO makes images findable in Google Images, understandable to search engines and screen readers, and light enough to load quickly on mobile data.

1. Write useful alt text

Alt text (the alt attribute) describes an image for people who can't see it, including screen reader users, and for search engines.

<img src="red-banarasi-silk-saree.webp" alt="Red Banarasi silk saree with gold zari border and pallu">

Good alt text:

  • describes what's in the image, specifically
  • is a short phrase or sentence, not a list of keywords
  • includes a keyword only when it naturally describes the image

Examples:

  • Weak: alt="saree", alt="image1", alt="saree silk saree buy saree online surat"
  • Good: alt="Green Kanjivaram silk saree with temple border"
  • Good: alt="Waterproofing membrane being applied on a terrace in Bopal"

Decorative images, such as background patterns or dividers, should have an empty alt, alt="", so screen readers skip them.

2. Name files clearly

Rename IMG_20260912_143201.jpg to red-banarasi-silk-saree.jpg before uploading. Use lowercase words separated by hyphens. It's a small signal, but it costs nothing.

3. Choose the right format

  • WebP: smaller than JPG and PNG at similar quality, and supported by all modern browsers. A good default for photos and graphics.
  • AVIF: even smaller in many cases, with growing support. Many image tools and CDNs serve it automatically.
  • JPG: fine for photos if WebP isn't an option.
  • PNG: for images that need transparency or sharp text, like screenshots.
  • SVG: for logos and icons, which stay sharp at any size.

4. Resize before you upload

A phone photo can be 4000 pixels wide and several megabytes. If it's displayed at 800 pixels wide, the visitor downloads five times more than needed. Resize images to roughly the largest size they're displayed at, and compress them. Free tools like Squoosh do both in the browser.

For responsive sites, srcset lets the browser pick the right size:

<img src="saree-800.webp" srcset="saree-400.webp 400w, saree-800.webp 800w, saree-1600.webp 1600w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 800px" alt="...">

WordPress and most modern platforms create these sizes automatically.

5. Always set width and height

Add width and height attributes so the browser reserves space before the image loads. Without them, text jumps down as images appear, which hurts your CLS score. Our Core Web Vitals guide explains why that matters.

6. Lazy-load below the fold, not above

loading="lazy" delays loading images until the visitor scrolls near them, which speeds up the first view. Use it on images further down the page, but not on the main image at the top. Lazy-loading the hero image delays your Largest Contentful Paint. For that image, use fetchpriority="high" instead.

7. Put images near relevant text

Google uses the text around an image, such as captions, headings and nearby paragraphs, to understand it. A product photo next to the product name and description is understood better than a gallery of unlabeled images.

8. Use real images

Original photos of your products, team and work are more convincing than stock photos, and they're unique, so they can rank in Google Images on their own.

9. Share images properly

For WhatsApp and social sharing, set an Open Graph image of 1200 × 630 pixels. For product pages, include images in Product schema.

Check your pages

The Rankdesk SEO audit lists every image on a page that has no alt text, and its PageSpeed results show which images are slowing the page down.

posts.title: How to Write an Instagram Bio That Gets Found and Followed
posts.description: Your Instagram name and bio decide whether people find you in search and whether they follow. A simple formula, examples by business and mistakes to avoid.

toc.text: Make the most of your link

posts.html:
When someone lands on your Instagram profile, they decide in a few seconds whether to follow, message you or leave. Your name field and bio do most of the work in those seconds. They also help people find you in Instagram search in the first place.

The two fields that matter

  • Name field: the bold name above your bio. It's searchable, so it should include what you do, not just your brand.
  • Bio: the short text under it, limited to 150 characters. It tells visitors what you offer and what to do next.

Your username (@handle) is searchable too, but changing it can confuse existing followers and break old links, so keep it stable once set.

The name field formula

Brand | What you do + City

  • Shree Textiles | Silk Sarees Surat
  • Bhanderi Buildcon | Builders Ahmedabad
  • Dr. Kavya Mehta | Dentist Vadodara
  • Crumbs & Co | Eggless Cakes Rajkot

If you sell online across India, swap the city for your main product detail: Loom Story | Handloom Cotton Sarees. Instagram limits how often you can change the name field, so decide carefully.

The bio formula

Three short lines usually work best:

  1. What you offer, in customer words, with a key detail
  2. Proof or location, such as city, years, delivery area or a credential
  3. A call to action pointing to your link, DMs or WhatsApp

Examples by business type

Manufacturer or wholesaler

Factory-direct pure silk sarees since 1998
📍 Surat · Ships across India
👉 DM "PRICE" for the wholesale list

Service business

House construction & renovation, on time
🏗 120+ homes built in Ahmedabad
📞 Free site visit, tap Call

Clinic

Painless dental care for the whole family
📍 Alkapuri, Vadodara · Open Sundays
🗓 Book your appointment below

Home bakery

Eggless custom cakes & dessert boxes
📍 Rajkot · Same-day delivery before 2 pm
👇 Order on WhatsApp

Online tool or app

Find any IP address location, free
⚡ City, ISP and map in one click
🔗 Try it at the link below

Emojis can make a bio easier to scan, but use them as signposts, not decoration. One per line is plenty.

Make the most of your link

You get a limited number of links in your bio. Point the main link to the page that matches your call to action, such as a WhatsApp chat, your product catalogue or a booking page, rather than always the home page. If you use a link-in-bio page with several links, keep it short and put the most important link first.

Use the other profile features

  • Category: choose the business category that fits best. It shows under your name.
  • Contact buttons: add call, email, WhatsApp and directions for a business account.
  • Story highlights: create highlights for products, prices, reviews, FAQs and how to order. They act like menu tabs on your profile.
  • Pinned posts: pin your best introduction, a customer review and your current offer.

Common mistakes

  • A name field with only the brand name, missing the chance to be found
  • A bio full of hashtags, which eats the few characters you have and sends visitors away to other people's posts
  • Vague lines such as "Living the dream ✨" for a business account
  • No call to action, so interested visitors don't know what to do
  • A broken or outdated link

Build yours

The Rankdesk hashtag generator writes a name field and bio from your brand, keywords and city, shows a profile preview and counts the characters. Then read our Instagram SEO guide to make your posts as findable as your profile.

posts.title: Product Schema for Online Stores: Price, Stock and Reviews
posts.description: Product structured data can show price, availability and ratings for your products in Google. The required fields, a full example and how to keep it accurate.
posts.html:
If you sell products online, Product schema is the structured data with the most visible payoff. It can let Google show your price, whether the item is in stock and its rating directly in search results and in Google's shopping features. Those details help shoppers choose your result before they click.

What Product schema can show

Depending on the page and the search, Google may show:

  • price and currency
  • availability, such as "In stock"
  • star rating and review count
  • shipping and return information
  • the product in Google's shopping surfaces

Google decides when to show these. Valid markup makes a page eligible, but doesn't guarantee it.

A complete example

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Product",
  "name": "Red Banarasi Silk Saree with Gold Zari",
  "image": [
    "https://shreetextiles.in/images/red-banarasi-front.jpg",
    "https://shreetextiles.in/images/red-banarasi-pallu.jpg"
  ],
  "description": "Handwoven pure silk Banarasi saree with gold zari border and matching blouse piece.",
  "sku": "BNR-RED-014",
  "brand": { "@type": "Brand", "name": "Shree Textiles" },
  "offers": {
    "@type": "Offer",
    "url": "https://shreetextiles.in/sarees/red-banarasi-silk",
    "price": "8499",
    "priceCurrency": "INR",
    "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock",
    "itemCondition": "https://schema.org/NewCondition"
  },
  "aggregateRating": {
    "@type": "AggregateRating",
    "ratingValue": "4.7",
    "reviewCount": "38"
  }
}

The fields that matter most

  • name: the product name as shown on the page.
  • image: one or more high-quality product photos. Google prefers several aspect ratios when available.
  • offers: the price block, with:
    • price: a number only, such as 8499, with no currency symbol or commas.
    • priceCurrency: INR for rupees.
    • availability: InStock, OutOfStock, PreOrder or BackOrder, as a schema.org URL.
  • description, sku, brand: help identify the product exactly.
  • gtin or mpn: if your products have barcodes (GTIN/EAN) or manufacturer part numbers, include them.
  • aggregateRating and review: only when real customer reviews are shown on the page.

Rules that keep it trustworthy

  1. Match the visible page. The price and stock in the markup must be what the shopper sees. If the page says ₹7,999 on sale, the markup can't say ₹8,499.
  2. Update it automatically. Prices and stock change. Markup generated by your store platform from your product data stays accurate. Hand-written markup goes stale.
  3. Real reviews only. Ratings must come from customers, be visible on the page, and not be selectively chosen.
  4. One product per product page. Category pages listing many products shouldn't mark each up as a full Product in the main position.

Platforms

  • Shopify: most themes output Product schema. Check it with the Rich Results Test, and avoid adding a second app that duplicates it.
  • WooCommerce: outputs Product schema, and SEO plugins can extend it.
  • Custom stores: generate the JSON-LD from the same data that renders the page, so they never disagree.

Merchant listings

Beyond schema, you can upload a product feed to Google Merchant Center, which can show your products in Google Shopping for free. Schema and the feed work together, and Merchant Center reports mismatches between them.

Test it

Use Google's Rich Results Test on a few product pages, and watch the Product snippets and Merchant listings reports in Search Console for errors such as "Missing field price" or "Invalid availability value".

The Rankdesk schema generator has a Product type with every field above and fills them from your page when you enter its URL. If you're new to structured data, start with schema markup for beginners.

posts.title: Noindex vs Robots.txt Disallow: The Difference That Breaks Sites
posts.seoTitle: Noindex vs Robots.txt Disallow: The Difference That Matters
posts.description: Robots.txt stops crawling and noindex stops indexing. Mixing them up can keep pages in Google you wanted gone, or remove ones you need. When to use each.

toc.text: Why a blocked page can still appear

posts.html:
"I blocked the page in robots.txt, so why is it still in Google?" It's one of the most common SEO questions, and the answer explains a mix-up that quietly breaks a lot of websites. Robots.txt and noindex sound like they do the same thing. They don't.

Two different jobs

Robots.txt Disallow noindex
What it controls Crawling: whether search engines may visit the page Indexing: whether the page may appear in search results
Where it lives One file at yourdomain.com/robots.txt A meta tag in the page, or an HTTP header
Can the page still appear in Google? Yes, if other pages link to it No, once Google sees the tag
Can Google read the page's content? No Yes

Why a blocked page can still appear

Robots.txt tells Google "don't visit this URL". It doesn't say "don't list it". If other pages link to the blocked URL, Google knows it exists and may still show it in results, usually with no description, because it was never allowed to read the page.

How noindex works

The noindex tag goes in the page's head:

<meta name="robots" content="noindex">

Or as an HTTP header, useful for PDFs and other files:

X-Robots-Tag: noindex

When Google crawls the page and sees it, the page is dropped from results.

The classic mistake

Combining both on the same page: noindex on the page and a robots.txt rule blocking it. Google can't crawl the page, so it never sees the noindex, and the page can stay in results indefinitely.

To remove a page from Google, let it be crawled and add noindex. Once it has dropped out of results, you can block it in robots.txt if you also want to save crawling, though for most small sites there's no need.

When to use robots.txt

  • Areas with no search value that could waste crawling: internal search results, endless filter combinations, cart and checkout
  • Admin and backend paths
  • Large sets of auto-generated URLs

When to use noindex

  • Thank-you and order confirmation pages
  • Thin pages you need for users but not in search, such as tag archives with one post
  • Internal campaign landing pages you don't want found organically
  • Staging copies of a site that must be reachable but not indexed (better still, password-protect them)

When to use neither

If a page shouldn't exist at all, delete it and return 404 or 410, or redirect it to a real replacement. If a page is a duplicate of another, use a canonical tag.

When to use a password

Anything private, such as client files, staff areas and unreleased products, needs real access control. Robots.txt is public and noindex only affects search engines. Neither stops a person who has the link.

The launch-day disaster

Many sites are built with "Discourage search engines" (WordPress) or a noindex tag on the staging site, plus Disallow: / in robots.txt. If either survives launch, the new site disappears from Google. Check both on launch day:

  1. Open yourdomain.com/robots.txt and make sure it doesn't say Disallow: /.
  2. In WordPress, Settings, Reading, make sure "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" is unticked.
  3. Audit the home page and a few key pages.

Removing a page urgently

If something sensitive is in Google, use the Removals tool in Search Console to hide it for about six months, then add noindex or remove the page permanently before that runs out.

Check any page

The Rankdesk SEO audit checks both: whether the page is blocked by robots.txt (and by which rule) and whether it has a noindex meta tag or header. Use the robots.txt generator to create a clean file, and read our robots.txt guide for the details.

posts.title: SEO-Friendly URLs: Short, Readable and Keyword-Focused
posts.description: A good URL tells people and search engines what a page is about before they click. The rules for readable URLs, what to avoid and how to change them safely.
posts.html:
A URL is the address of a page. Compare these two:

  • https://example.com/index.php?id=4821&cat=7
  • https://example.com/sarees/red-banarasi-silk

The second tells you what the page is before you open it. Search engines read URLs too, and people see them in search results, browser tabs and shared links. URLs are a small ranking factor, but they affect trust and clicks, and they're hard to change later, so it's worth getting them right from the start.

Rules for good URLs

1. Describe the page in a few words. /bathroom-waterproofing is clear. /services/our-premium-waterproofing-solutions-for-your-home is too long.

2. Use hyphens between words. Google treats hyphens as word separators. Underscores (red_silk_saree) and joined words (redsilksaree) are harder to read.

3. Lowercase only. URLs can be case-sensitive, so /Sarees and /sarees may be different pages. Lowercase avoids duplicates and broken links.

4. Include the main keyword naturally. /silk-sarees for a silk saree category. Don't repeat it: /silk-sarees/silk-saree-red-silk adds nothing.

5. Leave out filler. Words like "and", "the", "of" can usually go, as long as the URL still reads well.

6. Avoid dates in evergreen content. /blog/2026/10/how-to-choose-a-saree makes a timeless guide look old next year. /blog/how-to-choose-a-saree doesn't.

7. Keep a sensible structure. Folders can show hierarchy, such as /sarees/banarasi/red-silk. Don't go deeper than you need to. Two or three levels are plenty for most sites.

8. Use English letters for the main site. Hindi or Gujarati characters work in URLs, but they turn into long encoded strings when copied and shared, like %E0%A4%B8.... For local-language pages, a transliterated slug such as /hi/silk-saree is often easier to share. See our Hindi and Gujarati keywords guide.

What to avoid

  • Session IDs and tracking codes in normal links: ?sessionid=xyz. Use them only in campaign links and set a canonical tag on the page.
  • File extensions that reveal technology, like .php or .aspx. They're not harmful, but clean URLs age better if you ever change platforms.
  • Spaces and special characters, which become %20 and similar codes.
  • Keyword stuffing: /best-cheap-silk-saree-buy-online-silk-saree-surat.

Examples

Page Weak URL Better URL
Category /category.php?id=12 /sarees/banarasi
Product /product/8821 /sarees/red-banarasi-silk
Service /services/page-3 /waterproofing/terrace
Location /our-branch-in-vadodara-gujarat-india /branches/vadodara
Blog post /blog/2026/10/11/post-14 /blog/how-to-identify-pure-silk

Setting URLs in your platform

  • WordPress: Settings, Permalinks, choose "Post name". Edit each page's slug in the editor.
  • Shopify: the URL handle is in each product's search engine listing section. Shopify adds /products/ and /collections/ automatically.
  • Wix and Squarespace: edit the page URL or slug in each page's SEO settings.

Changing existing URLs

Changing a URL that already ranks or has links pointing to it carries risk. Only change it if the old URL is truly bad, and when you do:

  1. Set up a 301 redirect from the old URL to the new one. See 301 vs 302 redirects.
  2. Update internal links to point straight to the new URL.
  3. Update the sitemap.
  4. Re-check the old URL to confirm it redirects in one step.

For new pages, get the URL right the first time and leave it alone.

Check it

The Rankdesk SEO audit shows each page's final URL after any redirects, so you can spot messy addresses, and the meta tag generator previews how the URL appears in Google's result as a readable breadcrumb.

posts.title: Does Word Count Matter for SEO? What Actually Helps Pages Rank
posts.seoTitle: Does Word Count Matter for SEO? What Actually Helps
posts.description: There is no ideal word count for SEO. What Google actually rewards, why thin pages struggle, when long content wins and how to decide how much to write.

toc.text: How to decide how much to write
Quality signals that matter more than length

posts.html:
"How many words should a page have for SEO?" Ask five people and you'll hear 300, 1,000, 2,000 and "as many as possible". Google has said plainly that word count isn't a ranking factor. Yet thin pages really do struggle. Both are true, and understanding why helps you write the right amount.

Why there's no magic number

Google ranks pages by how well they meet the searcher's need. Some searches need one line: "Shree Textiles phone number". Others need a detailed guide: "how to start a saree business". Writing 2,000 words for the first wastes everyone's time. Writing 100 words for the second can't possibly cover it.

Long pages often rank well because covering a topic properly usually takes words, not because Google counts them.

Why thin pages struggle

A page with very little unique content gives Google little reason to show it:

  • It may not answer the question fully, so people go back to search.
  • It gives search engines few clues about what it covers.
  • Hundreds of near-empty pages, like product pages with one line, or city pages with only the city name changed, can make the whole site look low-value.

That's why the Rankdesk SEO audit flags pages with very little visible text. It isn't a rule. It's a prompt to check whether the page says enough.

How to decide how much to write

1. Look at what ranks. Search your keyword and open the top results. If they're all detailed guides, a short page won't compete. If they're product pages with a short description and lots of images, that's the format people want.

2. List the questions the page should answer. For a service page: what it is, who it's for, how it works, how long it takes, what it costs, why choose you, what to do next. Answer each one. That sets the length naturally.

3. Cut what doesn't help. Long introductions, repeated points and filler to reach a number make a page worse. Readers skim, and they leave when they can't find the answer.

Rough guide by page type

These aren't targets, just typical ranges for pages that do their job:

  • Contact page: short. Details, map and directions.
  • Product page: enough to describe the product fully, such as material, size, use, care and delivery, plus photos and reviews. Often 150 to 400 words of unique text.
  • Service page: usually 400 to 1,000 words, covering the questions above, with photos of real work.
  • Category page: a short introduction above the products, and optionally a buying guide below.
  • How-to guide: as long as the steps require. Often 800 to 2,000 words.

Quality signals that matter more than length

  • Answers early. Give the answer near the top, then the detail.
  • First-hand experience. Real photos, prices, examples, mistakes you've seen. Google's guidance emphasises content that shows real experience and expertise.
  • Structure. Clear headings, short paragraphs, lists and tables make longer pages easy to scan.
  • Accuracy and freshness. Update prices, laws, dates and screenshots.
  • Unique content. Copying manufacturer descriptions or competitors' text gives Google no reason to prefer your page.

Updating short pages

If an important page is thin:

  1. Add the questions customers ask about it, with clear answers.
  2. Add specifics: prices or ranges, timelines, materials, areas served.
  3. Add proof: photos, a short case study, reviews.
  4. Add an FAQ section at the end.
  5. Link to related guides and pages with internal links.

Then use keyword research to check the page covers the related searches people make.

The short version

Write as much as the reader needs and no more. If you've answered every question a customer would ask, the length is right.

posts.title: HTTPS and SEO: Moving a Small Site to SSL Without Losing Traffic
posts.seoTitle: HTTPS and SEO: Move a Small Site to SSL Safely
posts.description: HTTPS protects visitors and is a light ranking signal. How to get a free certificate, move from HTTP safely, fix mixed content and keep your rankings.

toc.text: Moving from HTTP to HTTPS safely

posts.html:
HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP, the protocol browsers use to load websites. It encrypts the connection between the visitor and your site, so passwords, form details and payment information can't be read or changed along the way. You can tell a site uses it by the https:// in the address.

Why it matters

  • Trust. Browsers mark HTTP pages as "Not secure", especially on pages with forms. Many visitors leave as soon as they see it.
  • Rankings. Google has used HTTPS as a ranking signal since 2014. It's a light signal, but there's no reason to give it away.
  • Features. Many modern browser features only work on HTTPS, and some referral data is lost when visitors move from an HTTPS site to an HTTP one.
  • Data. Without HTTPS, anyone on the same public Wi-Fi network could read or tamper with what's sent.

In short, every website needs HTTPS, even a simple brochure site.

Getting a certificate

HTTPS needs an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your hosting. It's usually free:

  • Most hosts offer free Let's Encrypt certificates with one click in the control panel, often turned on automatically.
  • Vercel, Netlify, Shopify, Wix and Squarespace include HTTPS automatically.
  • Cloudflare can add HTTPS in front of your site for free.

Paid certificates exist, but for most small business sites a free certificate provides the same encryption.

Moving from HTTP to HTTPS safely

1. Install the certificate and check https://yourdomain.com loads correctly.

2. Redirect all HTTP to HTTPS with permanent 301 redirects, page by page: http://example.com/sarees should go to https://example.com/sarees, not to the home page. Read 301 vs 302 redirects for why the type matters.

3. Pick www or non-www and redirect the other version too, so there's one address for every page. Avoid chains like http://example.com → https://example.com → https://www.example.com. Each old address should reach the final one in one step.

4. Update internal links in menus, content and templates to https://. WordPress users can change the site address in Settings, General, then use a search-and-replace plugin for old links in content.

5. Fix mixed content. If an HTTPS page loads images, scripts or styles over http://, browsers may block them or show a warning. Change those addresses to https://. Your browser's developer console lists mixed content errors.

6. Update canonical tags, the sitemap and robots.txt so they all use https:// addresses. See our guides to canonical tags and XML sitemaps.

7. Update Google Search Console. Add the HTTPS version as a property (a Domain property covers all versions at once) and submit the new sitemap.

8. Update external profiles, such as your Google Business Profile, social profiles and directories, to the HTTPS address.

Will rankings drop?

A careful move with page-by-page 301 redirects usually causes little or no lasting change. Search Console may show a short period of fluctuation while Google re-crawls. Rankings fall when redirects are missing, point to the home page, or go through long chains.

HSTS

Once everything works on HTTPS, you can add an HSTS header, which tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your site. It closes a small security gap. Only add it when you're sure, because browsers remember it, and removing HTTPS later becomes difficult.

Renewal

Free certificates usually last 90 days and renew automatically. If renewal fails, visitors see a full-page security warning. Most hosts email you before expiry. Don't ignore those emails.

Check your site

The Rankdesk SEO audit checks whether a page loads over HTTPS, follows the redirect chain from the address you entered, and flags temporary or multi-step redirects. Audit the http:// version of your home page to confirm it lands on the secure version in one step.

posts.title: The Free SEO Tools Every Beginner Should Use
posts.description: You can do most everyday SEO without paying for software. The free tools worth learning first, what each is for, and a simple weekly routine.
posts.html:
Paid SEO platforms are powerful, but they're built for agencies and large sites. For a small business or a new website, free tools cover almost everything you need: checking pages, finding keywords, watching performance and fixing problems. Here are the ones worth learning first.

The essentials

Google Search Console

What it does: shows how your site performs in Google search. Clicks, impressions, average position and the exact searches people used to find you. It also reports indexing problems, Core Web Vitals, mobile usability issues and security problems.

Why first: it's data straight from Google about your own site, and no other tool has it. Add your site, verify it and submit your sitemap.

Google Business Profile

What it does: your listing on Google Maps and local results, with calls, directions and reviews.

Why: for any business with local customers, it's often the biggest source of enquiries. See our setup guide.

Google PageSpeed Insights

What it does: measures how fast your pages load for real Chrome users and in a lab test, and lists what slows them down. Our Core Web Vitals guide explains the results.

Rankdesk

What it does: the SEO audit checks a page's titles, meta tags, headings, schema, redirects, robots.txt, sitemap and PageSpeed in one go. The generators write the fixes: meta tags, schema, hashtags and bios, keyword ideas, robots.txt and sitemaps.

For keyword research

  • Google Keyword Planner: search volume ranges and keyword ideas, free inside a Google Ads account, without running ads.
  • Google Trends: compare search interest over time and by state. Great for seasonal businesses.
  • Google autocomplete and "People also ask": real searches, straight from the results page.
  • AnswerThePublic: groups questions people ask around a keyword. The free tier has daily limits.

Read our keyword research guide for how to use them together.

For checking your work

  • Rich Results Test: confirms whether your schema qualifies for rich results.
  • Schema Markup Validator: checks any schema.org markup for errors.
  • Facebook Sharing Debugger and LinkedIn Post Inspector: preview and refresh how your links look when shared.
  • Bing Webmaster Tools: Search Console for Bing, which also feeds other search engines. It includes its own site scanner.

For whole-site checks and links

  • Screaming Frog SEO Spider: a desktop crawler that checks every page for broken links, missing titles, redirects and more. Free for up to 500 URLs, which covers most small business sites.
  • Ahrefs Webmaster Tools: free site audits and backlink data for sites you verify as your own.
  • Ahrefs Backlink Checker: a quick look at the top links to any site, including competitors.

For images

  • Squoosh: compress images and convert to WebP or AVIF in your browser. See our image SEO guide.

A simple weekly routine

Every week (15 minutes)

  1. Search Console: check clicks and impressions, and any new errors.
  2. Business Profile: reply to new reviews and questions.

Every month (1 hour)

  1. Audit your five most important pages.
  2. In Search Console, find searches where you rank on page two and improve those pages.
  3. Check PageSpeed for your home page and a key product or service page.

Every quarter

  1. Crawl the whole site with Screaming Frog for broken links and missing tags.
  2. Refresh your keyword list and plan new pages.

When to pay

Consider paid tools when you need rank tracking for many keywords, deep competitor research or backlink analysis across a whole industry. Until then, these free tools, used consistently, will take you a long way. Our directory of free SEO tools links to all of them.

posts.title: 15 Common SEO Mistakes on New Websites (and How to Fix Them)
posts.description: The SEO mistakes we see most often on new business websites, from launch-day noindex tags to missing titles and slow images, each with a quick way to fix it.
posts.html:
Most new websites don't fail because of advanced SEO problems. They fail on the basics, often things nobody noticed at launch. Here are the mistakes we find most often when auditing new business websites, roughly in order of how much damage they do.

Can Google see the site?

1. Search engines still blocked after launch

The development site had "Discourage search engines" ticked in WordPress, a noindex tag or Disallow: / in robots.txt, and it went live like that. The whole site stays out of Google.

Fix: check robots.txt and audit the home page on launch day. Read noindex vs robots.txt.

2. No HTTPS, or HTTP still working alongside it

Browsers show "Not secure", and Google may see two copies of every page.

Fix: install a free certificate and 301-redirect every HTTP URL. See HTTPS and SEO.

3. Old URLs not redirected after a redesign

The new site has new addresses, and every old link and ranking now leads to a 404.

Fix: map every old URL to its new one with 301 redirects. See 301 vs 302 redirects.

4. No Search Console

Without it, you won't know about indexing problems until traffic has already dropped.

Fix: set it up on day one and submit your sitemap.

Can Google understand it?

5. Titles like "Home" and "Untitled"

The title tag is the headline in Google results. Generic titles waste it.

Fix: give every page a unique title with its main keyword and, for local businesses, the city.

6. Missing or duplicate meta descriptions

Google picks random text, often the menu or a cookie notice.

Fix: write a unique description for each important page.

7. No H1, or the logo as the H1

Search engines and screen readers rely on headings to understand the page.

Fix: one clear H1 per page that says what it's about. See our headings guide.

8. One page for every service

A single "Services" page listing everything can't rank for each individual service.

Fix: create a page for each main service or product line.

9. Text inside images

Prices, offers and contact details baked into banner images can't be read by search engines or screen readers, and can't be copied.

Fix: put important text in real HTML text, and write alt text for every meaningful image.

Will people click and stay?

10. Huge images slowing the page

Uncompressed phone photos make pages slow on mobile data, and visitors leave.

Fix: resize, compress and convert to WebP. See Core Web Vitals.

11. Not built for mobile

Most local searches happen on phones. Tiny text, buttons too close together and pages wider than the screen drive people away.

Fix: test every page on a real phone, and make the phone number and WhatsApp link easy to tap.

12. No share image

Links shared on WhatsApp show no image, or a badly cropped logo.

Fix: add Open Graph tags with a 1200 × 630 image.

Will Google trust it?

13. Copied or thin content

Manufacturer descriptions copied word for word, or city pages identical except for the city name, give Google no reason to rank your page.

Fix: write original content with real details, photos and answers. See does word count matter.

14. No Google Business Profile, or inconsistent details

Local customers can't find you on Maps, or find an old address.

Fix: set up a Business Profile and make your name, address and phone match everywhere.

15. Buying links or "SEO packages" that promise page one

Cheap link packages and guaranteed rankings break Google's rules. At best they waste money, at worst they cause a penalty that takes months to undo.

Fix: earn links through partners, directories, local press and useful content. Be wary of anyone guaranteeing rankings.

Check your site in 20 seconds

The Rankdesk SEO audit catches mistakes 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 12 on any page, flags missing alt text (9) and a missing mobile viewport (11), and shows the redirect chain when you audit an old URL (3). Run it on your home page, a service or product page and a blog post, because each template can have different problems. For a step-by-step plan after that, read SEO for small businesses in India.
